veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The area and legal strength of marine protection created by the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill compared with pre-existing protections (Cape Rodney–Okakari Point and Whanganui A Hei marine reserves, cable protection zones, the 2000 Marine Park Act); true if the bill's protected area materially exceeds the prior total, false if prior protections equal or exceed it.

focus.statement: In May of this year, the current Minister for Oceans and Fisheries shelved those plans, and I want the other side of the House to really think about that, because we’ve heard in a number of these speeches and we see from all these reports that the Hauraki Gulf is protecting bits of the Hauraki Gulf.

veracity.statement: In November 2020, the High Court ruled that regulations 26 and 27 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 and the associated minimum standards in the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 were unlawful and invalid.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 2020 High Court holding: that regulations 26 and 27 of the 2018 Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations, and the associated minimum standards in the 2018 pigs code, were unlawful and invalid.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand High Court judgment in the 2020 judicial review brought by the New Zealand Animal Law Association and SAFE against the Attorney-General/Minister of Agriculture. veracity.statement: There are fewer than 80 farms, with around 45 indoor piggeries.

veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI or New Zealand Pork published counts of commercial pig farms and indoor piggeries for 2025. True if the total commercial farm count is below 80 and the indoor count is near 45; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The new confinement period, totalling seven days, is a significant reduction from the current 33-day setting, and will be amongst the lowest in the world, with most countries we currently import pork from allowing their use for 33 days.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable assertions: that the current New Zealand farrowing-crate limit is 33 days, and that most countries New Zealand imports pork from permit farrowing-crate confinement for 33 days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reg 26 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 for the 33-day New Zealand figure; and, for the comparison, the farrowing-crate rules of New Zealand's main pork-import sources (Stats NZ import-origin data, then EU Directive 2008/120/EC and the corresponding US/Canadian rules). True if the New Zealand limit is 33 days and the majority of import-source countries permit confinement of about that length or longer; false if the New Zealand figure is wrong or if most import sources permit materially shorter confinement.

specificity.statement: The bill limits the use of farrowing crates to a maximum of seven days—three days before and four days after farrowing.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is backing farmers, restoring balance, and making sure our regulations reflect both compassion and practicality.

specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: People in support of their use highlight lower piglet mortality due to crushing, and improved safety for farm workers while assisting sows and their piglets. Others, opposed to their use, are concerned about how they restrict sows from expressing normal behaviours.

rigor.statement: New Zealand Pork, MPI, and NZVA advised that confinement for no more than three days before and four days after farrowing, combined with the provision of manipulable and deformable materials during farrowing, meets the needs of the sow while also minimising piglet mortality.

The expertise is relevant to the question, which makes the appeal a reasonable one, but no evidence or mechanism is offered for why seven days is the point that balances sow welfare against piglet mortality, so a gap remains between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Without legislative action, there will be gaps in the law, gaps in particular about the requirements for how piglets and sows are managed during their most vulnerable stages of life.

focus.statement: The Animal Welfare Act does not permit an extension, and, unfortunately, that entire transition time was used when the industry had no idea what it was precisely supposed to transition towards.
focus.explanation: The one line in the speech that criticises the handling of the previous five years, and it stays on the policy: it names the statutory bar on extension and the specific failure — a transition period run without a defined destination. focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now that we’ve heard nearly 10 minutes of spin, let’s put some facts on the record today about why this bill is such a shocker and a terrible indictment on this House, on this Government’s lack of commitment to animal welfare.

civility.statement: Here’s my genuine olive branch: I will happily work with the Minister to extend what is currently in law by one or two years so we can get this right, but not reduce standards from what was consulted on in 2022 by such a massive reduction, and definitely not 10 years before we get minimal improvements in animal welfare for pigs—tiny improvements that the Minister is trying to stand up and claim as being a good thing.

veracity.statement: In 2018, the then Minister of Agriculture issued regulations and minimum standards, which allowed farrowing crates. veracity.statement: That’s the fundamental thing that this bill does: it delays the legislated action to bring an end to the cruel use of farrowing crates by 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill pushes the already-legislated end of farrowing crate use out by a further ten years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill and the commencement dates in the regulations it replaces. True if the bill moves the operative phase-out date roughly a decade beyond the existing 18 December 2025 deadline; false if the delay is materially shorter or the phase-out is not deferred.

veracity.statement: Guess who advised against that! The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, the very advisers to the Minister.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NAWAC's advice and recommendations to the Minister on the pig code of welfare and minimum space allowances, as published or released under the OIA. veracity.statement: It’s utterly unnecessary, because half of New Zealand pig farmers are already doing it like this, letting the pigs live a natural existence where they get to nurse their young and express their natural behaviours.

veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Pork or MPI figures on the proportion of New Zealand commercial pig farmers (or pigs farmed) using free-farrowing rather than farrowing crates. True if the share is around 50 percent; false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: I stand to speak on the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill and I just want to point out that, actually, we’ve lost a large number of our pork producers over the last three or four decades.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ agricultural production statistics and NZ Pork's count of commercial pig farms, comparing the mid-1980s/1990s with 2025. True if the number of commercial producers has fallen substantially; false if it has been broadly stable or risen.

veracity.statement: We, at the moment, in New Zealand import 60 percent of all our pork products from Canada or from the US or from over in Europe.

veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI/Stats NZ pork trade and consumption data on the imported share of pork consumed in New Zealand and the countries of origin. True if imports account for around 60 percent and the named countries are the main sources; false if the share is materially different.

specificity.statement: In 2018, the then Minister of Agriculture issued regulations and minimum standards, which allowed farrowing crates. Following that, the Labour Government put in place regulations to phase out farrowing crates by 18 December 2025.

specificity.statement: That’s the fundamental thing that this bill does: it delays the legislated action to bring an end to the cruel use of farrowing crates by 10 years.

specificity.statement: The bill recognised that achieving these improvements will require considerable adjustment from our farmers, many of whom have invested heavily in their current systems, and the bill also introduces a sensible transition period, allowing stakeholders time to adapt, plan, and invest in the necessary infrastructure. specificity.explanation: Describes a transition entirely in generic terms — "considerable adjustment", "a defined period", "the necessary infrastructure" — without naming the period, the standards, the costs or any support mechanism, in a debate where the ten-year timeframe is the contested point.

specificity.statement: We, at the moment, in New Zealand import 60 percent of all our pork products from Canada or from the US or from over in Europe.
specificity.explanation: A precise proportion attached to a named commodity and named source countries — directly checkable against trade statistics.

rigor.statement: The advice I’ve received from experts is that seven days will continue to put these animals at significant risk.

rigor.statement: It’s utterly unnecessary, because half of New Zealand pig farmers are already doing it like this, letting the pigs live a natural existence where they get to nurse their young and express their natural behaviours.

rigor.statement: It goes against the will of the New Zealand public, who were consulted extensively about their views of caging these animals like this, and their views were very clearly that it was not acceptable to them.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill seeks to establish clear, robust standards, setting minimum space requirements, improving the living environment, minimising the use of systems such as farrowing crates and gestation stalls, but over a period of time, because we’ve already lost a large number of our pork producers and the last thing we want to do is lose a large number more.

rigor.statement: As we’ve seen, across the floor, around the farrowing crates, yes, that is an issue, but it’s also an issue if they’re not used and young piglets are squashed.

focus.statement: Here’s my genuine olive branch: I will happily work with the Minister to extend what is currently in law by one or two years so we can get this right, but not reduce standards from what was consulted on in 2022 by such a massive reduction, and definitely not 10 years before we get minimal improvements in animal welfare for pigs—tiny improvements that the Minister is trying to stand up and claim as being a good thing.

veracity.statement: Just briefly to go back through history, the Animal Welfare Act was passed in 1999 by a visionary Government, a National Government actually, that saw the importance of animal welfare moving forward.

specificity.statement: The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, which is an independent committee, came up with a code of practice, a code of welfare, for pigs in 2010, again under a National-led Government.

specificity.statement: In fact, these new requirements in the bill will be among the highest animal welfare standards in the world.
specificity.explanation: A superlative comparison with no requirement, figure, date or jurisdiction named — the bill's actual content is never described, so there is nothing to act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The bizarre contradiction is that the pork industry has been lobbying the Government to say, “Don’t allow the importation of pork from lower-standard countries because we have higher standards.” Well, we’re moving to truly higher standards. This is going to dumb it down.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inconsistency argument: the industry's case against imports rests on having higher standards, which sits awkwardly with resisting the standards being raised. The inference tracks, though the middle step ('we're moving to truly higher standards') is asserted rather than shown, leaving a gap between the premise and the 'dumb it down' conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, of course, if you are changing regulations—and I know the other side of the House will say, “Well, Parliament is sovereign, and we can use Parliament’s resources to do this.”—what happens is that there is no recourse to the courts for judicial review for those regulations, for that secondary legislation.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the mechanism: moving regulatory content into primary legislation removes the judicial-review route that attaches to secondary legislation. She states and then answers the obvious counter (parliamentary sovereignty) rather than dodging it. Marked down slightly because the loss of review is asserted rather than sourced.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I’d say to this Government and to the Minister is that you’ve done the pork industry a disservice. Proposing this legislation might be giving them what they’re asking for, but it’s denying the reality of the direction of travel internationally.
civility.explanation: Directly addresses the Minister with a hard criticism, but the target is the legislative decision and its international consequences, not the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I put it to the House and the Minister that this is not an accident; it is a cynical use of the parliamentary process to stop citizens who are concerned about legislation not being followed.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Minister and the Government — the effect is described as deliberate and 'cynical'. Short of a personal insult, but it attributes motive rather than staying on the mechanism, which is a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the things that we were asked to do is that when the Government imposes the standards, make sure they are long term and enduring. This is not; this is halfway.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House on its own terms — the durability of the standard being set — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour is not supporting this bill, and we do not support this continued action by this Government to cynically override how regulatory processes are made and how they are able to be appealed.
focus.explanation: There is a real, named procedural point — changing regulations by primary legislation and the loss of appeal rights — but it is generalised into a pattern of conduct by 'this Government' rather than tied to a specific measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The committee received 210 written submissions, a relatively modest number in comparison to when Te Pūkenga was set up—I believe, from memory, there were about 2,000 submissions back then.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two counts: 210 written submissions to the Education and Workforce Committee on this bill, and roughly 2,000 written submissions on the legislation that established Te Pūkenga in 2019-20.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill states the number of written submissions received; the corresponding select committee report on the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill 2019 states its submission count. True if the reported figures are 210 and approximately 2,000 respectively; false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Without exception, they have all been pleased and relieved that they are getting their polytechnics back in their regions.
veracity.explanation: An absolute claim that every senior management team and community leader she met across the 10 institutes was pleased and relieved at the return of a regional polytechnic — i.e. that no one she met expressed reservations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, submissions to the Education and Workforce Committee, and media reporting from the councils, executives and community leaders of the 10 ITPs being stood up. True if none of those met recorded opposition or misgivings about the split from Te Pūkenga; false if any of them publicly expressed concern (for example over the financial viability of a standalone regional polytechnic).

rigor.statement: The vast majority of them were against the setting up of Te Pūkenga, so the 210 written submissions were relatively modest for this in comparison.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the stated premise (most 2019 submissions opposed Te Pūkenga) does nothing to support the conclusion drawn from it (that 210 submissions on this bill is a modest number by comparison). Submission volume and submission sentiment are unconnected quantities, and the 'so' joins them as if one followed from the other.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They will be statutory standard-setting bodies with majority of industry governance: six of the eight on the board will be from industry, ensuring that vocational education and training remains responsive to both new and emerging industry developments, as well as current industry needs.
specificity.explanation: Names the legal status of the new bodies and gives an exact governance composition (six of eight board members drawn from industry). Checkable against the bill; the trailing clause about responsiveness is generic, which is the only thing holding it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Therefore, I will bring an Amendment Paper to seek to change the commencement date of the bill, to ensure all preparation for the new system can be made prior to the proposed transfer date of 1 January 2026 and the new entities can be ready to operate from that date.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete legislative instrument (an Amendment Paper), the change sought (the commencement date), and a fixed date (1 January 2026). The new commencement date itself is not stated, which is the missing detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If there has been one thing that has come out of this adversity of Te Pūkenga, the one good thing has been that local communities have realised how important vocational education and training is, how important industry training is, and how important polytechnics are to their regions.
focus.explanation: Aimed at a named policy (the Te Pūkenga amalgamation) and its effect on regions rather than at the party that created it. Held below the top only because the content is a general reflection on community sentiment rather than a mechanism, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If there has been one thing that has come out of this adversity of Te Pūkenga, the one good thing has been that local communities have realised how important vocational education and training is, how important industry training is, and how important polytechnics are to their regions.
civility.explanation: A contested reform where the opportunity to turn on the previous government was plainly available. The criticism lands entirely on the policy — 'this adversity of Te Pūkenga' — and no person is impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Only 11 percent of submitters supported this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure for the share of submitters to the Education and Workforce Committee who supported the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill. Later in the same speech he restates it as 11 percent who 'unconditionally backed' the reforms, so the operative claim is the proportion of submissions recorded as supportive.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee report and the Ministry of Education departmental report on submissions to the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if the tallied share of submitters expressing support is approximately 11%, false if the recorded share is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Minister repeatedly says that Te Pūkenga was not financially viable, despite it returning a $16.7 million surplus last year, as it was intended to do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga reported a surplus of $16.7 million in its most recent financial year, and that this was in line with its planned financial trajectory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's audited annual report / financial statements for the 2024 financial year; true if the reported net surplus is approximately $16.7 million, false if it recorded a deficit or a materially different surplus.

veracity.statement: We’ve already lost 19,000 construction workers, and last year, 3,700 fewer individuals enrolled in building apprenticeships and there were 9,000 overall fewer apprentice completions across all fields year on year under this National Government.
veracity.explanation: Three separate quantitative claims: a fall of 19,000 in construction employment, 3,700 fewer building apprenticeship enrolments in the prior year, and 9,000 fewer apprenticeship completions across all fields year on year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment series (HLFS/filled jobs) for the period since late 2023, and Tertiary Education Commission industry training and apprenticeship enrolment/completion statistics for 2024 vs 2023; true if each figure matches those series within rounding, false if any is materially overstated or reversed in direction.

veracity.statement: The Minister, in fact, promised industry a stronger role under these reforms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Penny Simmonds publicly committed that industry would have a stronger leadership role under the vocational education reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial press releases, the vocational education reform consultation documents and Cabinet papers issued by Penny Simmonds from 2024 onward; true if she publicly committed to a stronger or leading role for industry in the redesigned system, false if no such commitment is on record.

specificity.statement: Consultants have indicated that $190 million may be needed to restart the 16 polytechnics, and yet there’s only a minimum of $177 million in Government funding set aside to support this.
specificity.explanation: Two named dollar figures against a named count of institutions, with the gap between requirement and appropriation made explicit. Someone could check both numbers against the consultants' advice and the Budget appropriation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve already lost 19,000 construction workers, and last year, 3,700 fewer individuals enrolled in building apprenticeships and there were 9,000 overall fewer apprentice completions across all fields year on year under this National Government.
specificity.explanation: Three checkable figures attached to named cohorts and a stated comparison period. Precise enough that anyone could look each number up.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Consultants have indicated that $190 million may be needed to restart the 16 polytechnics, and yet there’s only a minimum of $177 million in Government funding set aside to support this.
rigor.explanation: A straightforward inference: if the restart cost is $190m and only $177m is set aside, the funding falls short. The arithmetic follows from the premises; the gap is that 'may be needed' and 'minimum of' are soft on both sides, so the shortfall is asserted more firmly than the stated numbers support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: ISBs don’t have the powers industry has asked for and they don’t have the funding that they need under this legislation—$30 million is not enough to do the same job that workforce development councils were doing for $60 million.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a halving of funding ($60m to $30m) to inadequacy of the new bodies. The inference is reasonable but rests on an unstated premise that industry skills boards carry exactly the same functions as workforce development councils; if the scope narrowed, the comparison does not carry the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This legislation is resulting in more job cuts, more programmes lost, and more campuses closing as a result of Minister Simmonds’ and the National Government’s choices.
civility.explanation: Names the Minister and attributes the outcome to her choices, but the attack lands entirely on the decision and the legislation, not on her character or competence. Hard criticism of a policy is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m unsure if she even listened to the recommendations in that report.
civility.explanation: Moves from the substance of the select committee report to a suggestion that the Minister personally did not bother to read or heed it — an imputation about her conduct rather than a criticism of the legislation. Short of an insult, but no longer purely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What we do see in the changes post select committee is a further reduction, though, of Māori representation, and some over the other side will be happy about this. This is what they voted for.
civility.explanation: Imputes to members opposite that they will be pleased by a reduction in Māori representation, i.e. attributes a motive rather than engaging their stated reasons. Aimed at a group rather than a named individual, so short of a personal attack, but it is an imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This legislation is resulting in more job cuts, more programmes lost, and more campuses closing as a result of Minister Simmonds’ and the National Government’s choices.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and its named consequences — job cuts, programme losses, campus closures. Attributing them to the responsible Minister and government is accountability for a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we do see in the changes post select committee is a further reduction, though, of Māori representation, and some over the other side will be happy about this. This is what they voted for.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — a specific change made after select committee reducing Māori representation requirements — but half the statement is framing about what the other side wanted and voted for, rather than about the provision itself.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m hearing every week from the sector that these cuts and closures are only going to increase under this reform.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the rate of job cuts, programme cancellations and campus closures across the polytechnic sector will rise following the reform, rather than stabilise.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and individual polytechnic announcements of redundancies, programme discontinuations and site closures in the 12 months after October 2025, compared with the preceding 12 months; true if the counts rise, false if they hold steady or fall.

focus.statement: One of the things that this bill has failed to do is it has failed to guarantee any kind of staff or student representation on the governing councils of the newly established institutes of technology and polytechnic (ITP) councils.
focus.explanation: Names a specific gap in the measure before the House — council composition and representation of staff and students. Squarely on the policy mechanism, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Instead of fixing that issue, what the previous Government—the Labour Government—did was they decided to come up with this idea of a mega-merger.
focus.explanation: A named policy (the Te Pūkenga mega-merger) and a real policy claim — that it was pursued instead of addressing sector decline. But the weight of the passage is on characterising the previous Government's motives rather than on the merger's effects, so it sits between accountability and party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to highlight two changes which ACT managed to get in this legislation: one is in new section 318, inserted by clause 22, which is about “Matters to be considered when appointing members of polytechnic’s council”.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the content of the measure before the House: a specific clause and what it governs. No party-versus-party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, the Treasury analysis of this reform said that the newly established ITPs could expect financials that were the same, if not worse, than before Te Pūkenga was established.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury's published analysis of the vocational education reform forecast the new ITPs' financial position as no better, and possibly worse, than the pre-Te Pūkenga baseline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury / MoE Regulatory Impact Statement and Treasury's advice on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill: true if it states the disestablished ITPs' expected financial position is equal to or worse than pre-2020; false if Treasury forecast improved financials or made no such comparison.

veracity.statement: There were 855 job losses last year and 1,000 are expected in this year.
veracity.explanation: Two numeric claims about job losses in the polytechnic sector: 855 in the prior year (2024) and roughly 1,000 forecast for the current year (2025).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC/Te Pūkenga workforce reporting and Tertiary Education Union redundancy tallies for 2024 and 2025: true if the 2024 figure is 855 ± rounding and the 2025 forecast is around 1,000; false if the counts are materially different.

veracity.statement: We do know that the Government has withdrawn from proposals to close the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses, thanks to the efforts made by communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that closure proposals for the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses were formally withdrawn.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Toi Ohomai / Te Pūkenga change-proposal decision documents and Ministry of Education announcements for 2025: true if the final decisions retain the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses after they had been proposed for closure; false if closure proceeded or was never proposed.

veracity.statement: This Government has talked about how they want to reduce the amount of people—particularly young people—going on to be beneficiaries, but the free TAFE programme in Australia shows that when someone has gone through the free TAFE programme, they’re 37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit, and over half of those people who have gone through the free TAFE programme have actually seen their incomes increase.
veracity.explanation: Two statistical claims about outcomes of the Australian Free TAFE programme: a 37 percent reduction in likelihood of benefit receipt, and more than half of participants experiencing income increases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian Department of Employment and Workplace Relations Free TAFE evaluation/outcome reporting and NCVER student outcomes surveys: true if a published evaluation reports a ~37% lower rate of income-support receipt and >50% of completers with increased income; false if the published figures differ materially or no such finding exists.

veracity.statement: Look, the Minister talks about how this is an industry-centred reform, but, actually, of the around 38 industry submitters, only eight of them gave their full support to the changes.
veracity.explanation: A count of the select committee submissions: approximately 38 submitters identifiable as industry, of whom only 8 expressed full support for the bill's changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's published submissions on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill: true if roughly 38 industry submissions were received and about 8 recorded unqualified support; false if the counts differ materially.

specificity.statement: There were 855 job losses last year and 1,000 are expected in this year.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures tied to named years. Anyone could go and check them against workforce reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has talked about how they want to reduce the amount of people—particularly young people—going on to be beneficiaries, but the free TAFE programme in Australia shows that when someone has gone through the free TAFE programme, they’re 37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit, and over half of those people who have gone through the free TAFE programme have actually seen their incomes increase.
specificity.explanation: A named overseas programme with two quantified outcome measures. Checkable and directly usable as an argument for a policy transfer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would like to highlight two changes which ACT managed to get in this legislation: one is in new section 318, inserted by clause 22, which is about “Matters to be considered when appointing members of polytechnic’s council”.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision — new section 318, inserted by clause 22 — and its subject matter. Anyone can locate and check the change in the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Contrary to the Minister for Vocational Education’s rhetoric about how they’re overstaffed, for a sector that had only about 8,000 staff, losing about one-seventh of the staff is absolutely devastating to the capacity of these regions, and also the capacity of these institutions to remain as ongoing and viable concerns.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: given a base of ~8,000 staff, the stated losses are a large proportion, and a large proportional workforce loss plausibly reduces institutional capacity. The conclusion tracks the premise; the gap is that 'devastating' and the viability claim are asserted rather than shown, and no mechanism links headcount to viability.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think by just focusing on gender and ethnicity, we are not going to deliver what polytechs should be delivering.
rigor.explanation: Engages the actual appointment provision, but the inference rests on a strawman: the removed subclauses listed gender and ethnicity among several considerations, not as the sole criterion, so 'just focusing on' misdescribes the position being refuted. The conclusion about delivery is then asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the offer that I’m going to make to the Minister—which I’m not going to make through some botched hit job through the media, like the Prime Minister did with the energy reform hit job, and the more successful hit job that Erica Stanford did—is that we do want to work with the Government on an actual cross-party tertiary strategy that will actually endure a change of Government, because when the election happens next year and, God willing, I end up as the tertiary education Minister, I don’t want to have to rip up what’s already been done before.
civility.explanation: The substantive offer is constructive, but it is framed by characterising two named individuals' conduct as a 'botched hit job' — imputing bad faith and a sneer at the Prime Minister's competence. Short of a direct insult, but past the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because that is just empty virtue signalling, and we don’t believe in that.
civility.explanation: 'Empty virtue signalling' imputes insincerity to the members holding that position rather than engaging their reason for it. Dismissive of motive rather than argument — a real failure, though short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m not able to discuss it because it’s still in the middle of a media pitch, but when it does come out, it will reveal that, actually, this thing is not that financially viable.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a later, as-yet-unreleased piece of Treasury advice, once public, will show the vocational education reform is not financially viable.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Treasury advice on the vocational education reform released after 7 October 2025 (proactive release or OIA): true if the released advice states or clearly implies the reformed ITP model is not financially viable; false if it finds the model financially viable or the advice is never released.

focus.statement: Now, Labour loved centralisation. I think that’s unarguable. I mean, we had that in health, we had that in the water sector, and we had that in education at the very least.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — three named sectors where restructuring happened — but the framing is a characterisation of the other party's disposition rather than of a measure, cost or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New section 367, inserted by clause 23, sets out a range of important functions which, actually, if you look at them, are basically the same as the WDCs, but it also takes over the actual training process.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the bill before the House — a named clause and what it does — with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the Green Party will probably say, “Well, just tax the living daylights out of everybody.” That’s a guaranteed way of making sure we’ll actually all end up poorer.
focus.explanation: The underfunding question is a genuine policy issue, but the response is directed at an imagined position of another party rather than at any funding mechanism or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Anyway, Labour established Te Pūkenga, as we know, by merging 16 polytechs and nine workplace training providers, and that only really started operating at the beginning of 2023.
specificity.explanation: Two counts and a start date attached to a named entity; anyone could go and check the merger composition and the commencement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New section 367, inserted by clause 23, sets out a range of important functions which, actually, if you look at them, are basically the same as the WDCs, but it also takes over the actual training process.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause and the inserted section, and states precisely what changes relative to the WDCs' existing functions.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we have to do is we have to earn more money as a country so that we can afford the quality public services that we need, and that includes education. We need to lift productivity. That’s been a long-term blight on our country. We need to stop getting in our own way. We need to reform our resource management and other bureaucratic processes.
specificity.explanation: A chain of directions — earn more, lift productivity, reform resource management — with no mechanism, no figure and no timeframe attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Anyway, Labour established Te Pūkenga, as we know, by merging 16 polytechs and nine workplace training providers, and that only really started operating at the beginning of 2023.
veracity.explanation: Three assertions in one: that Labour created Te Pūkenga, that it merged 16 polytechs plus nine workplace training providers, and that it only began operating properly in early 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC / Te Pūkenga establishment records and the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Act 2020: true if 16 institutes of technology and polytechnics and nine industry training organisations' training arms were merged into Te Pūkenga, and if it began operating as a single unified entity at the start of 2023; false if the counts differ materially or the unified operating date is a different year.

veracity.statement: Te Pūkenga was based in Hamilton.
veracity.explanation: A factual correction to the claim that Te Pūkenga's bureaucracy sat in Wellington — asserting the organisation's national office was in Hamilton.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's registered head office address in the Companies Office / Crown entity records and its annual report: true if the national office was located in Hamilton, false if it was in Wellington or elsewhere.

rigor.statement: These are the things, Shanan Halbert, that I actually heard from people in the comments. I didn’t get to sit in the select committee, but I certainly hear these kind of things around the country as I meet with people.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: challenged on a factual point, the support offered for the claims about lost regional autonomy and politicised WDCs is what the speaker has personally heard, with no submission, survey or report cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the Green Party will probably say, “Well, just tax the living daylights out of everybody.” That’s a guaranteed way of making sure we’ll actually all end up poorer.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: a caricatured position is put into the Greens' mouths and then refuted, and the refutation itself ('guaranteed' to make everyone poorer) is a bare assertion with no mechanism or evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We had a question today about why some people are leaving our country. Well, in some cases, it’s because we are driving them out of the country. That, I put on the previous Government—and we’re trying to fix that problem.
rigor.explanation: Causal attribution asserted without support: emigration is pinned on the previous Government with no data, mechanism or intermediate step offered connecting the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Having actually sat on the board—the council—of a regional polytechnic, I appreciate the value of local input into ensuring polytechs that deliver education in our regions. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: The 'therefore' rests entirely on personal experience: an appeal to the speaker's own authority and anecdote, with nothing connecting board service to the merits of this bill's governance model.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Te Pūkenga might have been founded with good intentions, but poor delivery and the lack of regionalisation, the bureaucracy sitting in Wellington—not a good model.
civility.explanation: A blunt verdict on the model — poor delivery, wrong structure — that concedes good intentions and attacks no person; hard criticism of a policy is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I'm really disappointed in some of the arguments that I'm hearing here tonight, that this is going to see local decision-making. Local decision-making is already happening. What it means for local decision-making is that courses are being cut, whole sites are being cut.
rigor.explanation: A genuine counter-argument to the bill's central claim, but it equivocates on 'local decision-making': the devolution the bill proposes and the cost-driven course cuts happening under the current structure are treated as the same thing, so the conclusion that devolution means cuts is not established by what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because the locals know what they want, they're going to stand it up. It will work. It will be much better than a Te Pūkenga.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion 'it will work' rests entirely on the premise that locals know what they want. Local preference is asserted as sufficient for institutional viability with nothing offered to connect them — a non sequitur, and the comparative claim against Te Pūkenga is bare assertion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Pick the region, pick the media outlet, pick the industry—they've all got criticisms because there is no clear plan.
rigor.explanation: Infers the absence of a plan from the breadth of criticism. That is an appeal to popularity — widespread objection to a policy is consistent with many causes and does not establish the specific defect concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I'm really disappointed in some of the arguments that I'm hearing here tonight, that this is going to see local decision-making. Local decision-making is already happening. What it means for local decision-making is that courses are being cut, whole sites are being cut.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific mechanism the bill is said to deliver — local decision-making — and what it produces in practice. Squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can that side of the House sit there when you've got the likes of Tokoroa, who are going to lose their whole site? A Government who has sat blindly on the side of seeing absolutely massive cuts in jobs in that town, watching a whole town become an absolute ghost town—that is on that Government.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy outcome named — the loss of the Tokoroa site and the jobs attached to it — but a good part of the weight is on 'that side of the House' sitting blindly, which is party framing rather than policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Hon Penny Simmonds promised the industry a stronger role and a more responsive vocational system. This is a broken promise, and the industry has spoken out strongly against these reforms.
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment made about the reform and tests the reform against it. This is scrutiny of a named policy promise, not party-bashing, and is exactly the job of an opposition MP.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We hear very little about this, but we know from what's been in the media recently that there has been a release of information that shows that this is going to cost a lot more than what they were absolutely telling us it was going to cost.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an information release reported in the media shows the transition cost of the vocational education reforms exceeds the figure the Government had previously stated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reporting (RNZ/NZ Herald) in September–October 2025 on an official information release covering the cost of the Te Pūkenga disestablishment/transition, compared against the Government's earlier published transition cost estimate; true if the released figure materially exceeds the earlier stated figure, false if no such release exists or it is at or below the earlier figure.

veracity.statement: The member for Northland said, in an RNZ article, that the Government has no intention whatsoever to close NorthTec, and he promises that.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to the MP for Northland: that in an RNZ article he stated the Government has no intention of closing NorthTec. What is checkable is whether he said it, not whether NorthTec closes.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ coverage of the vocational education reforms in 2025 quoting the MP for Northland on NorthTec's future; true if he is quoted saying the Government has no intention of closing NorthTec, false if no such quote appears or the quote is materially different.

veracity.statement: There was 11 percent support for this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 11 percent of submitters on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill supported the proposal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the bill, or the departmental report's summary of submissions; true if the proportion of submitters recorded as supporting the proposal is approximately 11 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: As of last year, some 900 fulltime-equivalents, 500 programmes, and approximately 30 delivery sites have been cut—cut, cut, cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that across the vocational education sector roughly 900 full-time-equivalent positions, 500 programmes and about 30 delivery sites were cut as at 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and Te Pūkenga / polytechnic reporting on staffing, programme and site reductions during 2024, or the Tertiary Education Union's tally; true if the aggregate figures are close to 900 FTE, 500 programmes and 30 sites, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: In fact, we saw in yet another article, the RNZ article, that there's an estimate of about $190 million, more than the total amount allocated to the Government for transition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that RNZ reported an estimated transition cost of about $190 million for the vocational education reforms, exceeding the total funding allocated for the transition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ reporting in 2025 on the cost of disestablishing Te Pūkenga, checked against the transition funding appropriated in Budget 2024/2025; true if a figure of approximately $190 million is reported and exceeds the appropriation, false if no such figure appears or it is within the allocated amount.

specificity.statement: Let me tell you what's happening in Northland and why these changes are so important for my region: we are looking to stand up a polytech that will be enduring, that will serve our region, and that will look after the people in the North.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the substantive case for the change, but it is a string of generic virtues — enduring, serves the region, looks after people — with no courses, campuses, student numbers, funding or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As of last year, some 900 fulltime-equivalents, 500 programmes, and approximately 30 delivery sites have been cut—cut, cut, cut.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, checkable quantities with a stated period — FTE roles, programmes and delivery sites cut. Someone could go and verify each.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, I actually think right from the beginning of this legislation, this was a campaign issue for the Minister. This has been a personal vendetta, and today, here we are, another step in the process of achieving the Minister's goal of overturning—the flip-flopping.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual: the legislation is characterised as the Minister pursuing a personal vendetta rather than a policy judgement. That is an attack on motive, not on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There are going to be more cuts.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that further reductions — staffing, programmes or delivery sites — will occur in the vocational education sector following the bill's passage. Not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Announcements by the new standalone polytechnics, the Tertiary Education Commission, or Tertiary Education Union tallies covering the period after October 2025; true if further staff, programme or campus reductions are announced across the sector, false if the sector records no net further cuts through the resolve-by date.

focus.statement: It seems to be flip-flopping that’s based on vanity, and it’s vindictive and it’s full of lazy terms.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's motives — vanity, vindictiveness — rather than engaging any provision of the bill. No policy, figure or outcome is named. Nobody is personally insulted, so this is a Focus failure, not a Civility one. No argument survives once the party-characterisation is removed, so nothing is emitted for Rigor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The point is that we have not heard arguments for why it is that the Government members are so opposed to the Education and Training Act as it stands and why they are so opposed to workforce development councils.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: names the Act and the specific bodies being replaced, and demands the government's case for changing them. Legitimate scrutiny, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My point here is that we have heard over and over from the other side of the House that this is somehow all about local control. But I ask you, for Otago Polytechnic, how is it possibly about local control when it is not that anchor polytech?
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's federation mechanism and tests the government's stated purpose against it. Names a specific institution and a specific structural feature.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now he’s informing the House that, in fact, he didn’t not say that they weren’t ideological. Work that sentence out, Hansard.
civility.explanation: Mockery of another member's correction, played as a joke about his double negative. It edges toward the person without landing on his character or competence — pointed rather than abusive.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is very interesting that you would put someone who has such strong desires to break up polytechs and to bring back SIT at any cost—that it is going to be difficult for that Minister to look at the evidence and make good decisions.
civility.explanation: Imputes to the Minister a personal agenda pursued 'at any cost' and an inability to weigh evidence. It stops short of a direct insult but attributes bad faith to the individual rather than criticising the decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is a shameful bill and it’s terrible for Dunedin.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation aimed entirely at the bill and its regional effect. No person is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to an individual — harsh about the measure is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So we heard Andy Foster say that they were ideological.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Andy Foster, in his speech on this bill, described workforce development councils as ideological in his own voice. Foster disputes this in the chamber, saying he reported others' views.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of Andy Foster's speech on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, 7 October 2025: true if he characterises workforce development councils as ideological as his own view; false if he only reports that others told him they were ideological.

veracity.statement: I know that because I recall her huge opposition to the mergers of the polytechs. She was very vocal about that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Minister, while chief executive of the Southern Institute of Technology, publicly and vocally opposed the amalgamation of polytechnics into Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous public record 2018–2020 — select committee submissions on the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill, SIT media releases, and news coverage: true if the SIT chief executive is on record repeatedly opposing the merger, false if no such public opposition is documented.

veracity.statement: So it seems that this Government is down on Dunedin, it is down on jobs, and we’ve had reports in the Otago Daily Times that the polytech might have to decrease their land area by 60 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Otago Daily Times has reported that Otago Polytechnic may have to reduce its land area by around 60 percent. The checkable core is the existence and content of that reporting, not the 'down on Dunedin' framing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Daily Times reporting during 2025 on Otago Polytechnic's campus footprint: true if an ODT article reports a prospective reduction of roughly 60 percent in the polytechnic's land area, false if no such figure appears or the reported figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: This is very interesting that you would put someone who has such strong desires to break up polytechs and to bring back SIT at any cost—that it is going to be difficult for that Minister to look at the evidence and make good decisions.
rigor.explanation: A genuine conflict-of-interest inference — prior institutional attachment, now decision-making power over the same institutions — which is a legitimate structural argument, not a bare ad hominem. But the step from 'strong desires' to 'will not look at the evidence' is asserted rather than shown, and no instance of evidence being ignored is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My point here is that we have heard over and over from the other side of the House that this is somehow all about local control. But I ask you, for Otago Polytechnic, how is it possibly about local control when it is not that anchor polytech?
rigor.explanation: A valid tension argument: the government's stated rationale is local control; the bill's federation structure subordinates Otago Polytechnic to an anchor polytechnic elsewhere; therefore the rationale does not hold for this case. The premises are drawn from the clauses she has just traced, and the conclusion follows from them.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is returning autonomy to the regions, as has been described, but also setting up a very useful system to allow for federation, which will keep long-term sustainability, it will enable cost-effective delivery, and it will be a very useful system.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — autonomy, sustainability, cost-effectiveness, 'very useful' twice — with no figures, timeframes, named institutions or description of how the federation mechanism achieves any of them. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the biggest changes, I think, is that these small houses got bigger. They’re now 65 to 70 square metres and I think that’s fantastic.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific change made by the select committee and gives a concrete floor-area figure that could be checked against the reported-back bill. Marked down from the top because it is stated as a loose range rather than a single threshold, and no other parameter (commencement, cost, conditions) is supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Things like a project information memorandum, or PIM, making it easier to process; clarifying key phrases, defining them—that’s actually really important legislative work that the select committee’s been doing because, ultimately, we want to make sure this bill is effective, is easy for builders, for homeowners, for landowners to be able to use.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names a specific instrument in the bill (the project information memorandum) and the drafting work done on definitions, and identifies who the change is meant to serve. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is one of the most popular pieces of legislation, I think, that this Government is implementing. I know how many people in my electorate come up to me and talk to me about this piece of legislation, and how excited they are, so I just want to say thank you to the select committee for all of the incredibly important changes you’ve made.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a claim about the legislation's popularity across the country is supported only by unquantified reports of constituents approaching the speaker in his own electorate. Self-selected encounters with a minister in a single seat do not license a conclusion about national popularity. The inference is about the policy rather than about opponents, so it is a genuine Rigor item.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The select committee also recommended that a new section is inserted to ensure that implied warranties, which are an existing consumer protection mechanism under the Building Act, continue to be applied, because, of course, we also need to make sure that we are protecting consumers, protecting those people who will become the owners of these properties, as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts: that implied warranties are an existing consumer-protection mechanism in the Building Act, and that the Transport and Infrastructure Committee recommended inserting a new section so those warranties continue to apply to dwellings built under this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Building Act 2004 (subpart 6 of Part 4A, the implied warranties provisions, ss 362I–362K) and the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Building and Construction (Small Standalone Dwellings) Amendment Bill. True if implied warranties are an existing Building Act consumer-protection mechanism AND the committee's report recommends a new section preserving their application; false if either limb is absent from those documents.

divination.statement: These changes will increase the supply of affordable housing options and provide Kiwis with more choices.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a market outcome — that the consenting exemption for small standalone dwellings will raise the supply of affordable housing options — rather than promising an action by the speaker. The bill's passage is the speaker's own action; the resulting change in housing supply is not.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE building consent data and the exemption/notification records for small standalone dwellings (up to 70 square metres) for the two years after the Act commences, compared with the two years before. True if the annual count of such dwellings built rises materially above the pre-commencement baseline; false if the count is flat or falls.

civility.statement: Did you just arrive? Oh, sorry, have you been here the whole time?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mockery aimed at another member's attendance rather than at anything they argued. It stops short of a direct insult but is sneering and personal, which is a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister has promised so much in terms of these reforms, but the information just isn’t even there. We can’t see the plan. We can’t see how they’re going to be financially viable.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the reform package and its financial documentation — legitimate scrutiny of a named Minister's programme, not party-bashing. Slightly short of 1.0 because no particular figure or document is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Te Pūkenga was a failed Labour experiment. Big Brother. Centralisation.
focus.explanation: A named policy (Te Pūkenga) is the nominal subject, but the content is party labelling — 'Labour experiment', 'Big Brother' — with no mechanism, cost or outcome attached. Mostly framing, some policy anchor.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They talk about the regional campuses being cut and the financial risk is being offloaded to communities that are already under-resourced.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the consequences of the measure before the House — campus closures and where the financial risk lands — citing the departmental report rather than characterising the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister has promised so much in terms of these reforms, but the information just isn’t even there. We can’t see the plan. We can’t see how they’re going to be financially viable.
specificity.explanation: The complaint is that detail is absent, but the statement itself supplies none: no plan, cost, or modelling document is named, and 'the information' is left undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill brings polytechs back to the community, puts the “local” back in local, is community-led, focused on community needs, and enables viability into the future.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — community-led, community needs, viability — with no governance mechanism, funding figure, timeframe or named institution. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They know it is going to lead to job cuts, to cuts to courses, to the sale of land that we won’t be able to get back, and they’re just agreeing with their Minister and saying that this is going to be a great thing and promising.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the vocational education reforms will produce staff redundancies, course closures and disposal of institute land in the regions. Not a promise about the speaker's own action, so it is a prediction rather than a commitment.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Public announcements, annual reports and TEC records for the regional institutes of technology and polytechnics created on disestablishment of Te Pūkenga: true if redundancies, programme/course closures and sales of campus land are recorded at regional institutes following the reform; false if the new institutes complete the transition without redundancies, course closures or land sales.

veracity.statement: It resulted in $300 million going down the gurgler—$300 million down the Labour fiscal drain.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga consumed or lost approximately $300 million of public money over its existence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's audited annual reports 2020–2024 and Tertiary Education Commission funding/deficit records: true if cumulative operating deficits plus establishment/transition costs attributable to Te Pūkenga total approximately $300 million; false if the audited figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Well, I’m assuming most of the members know that the head office for Te Pūkenga actually is in the Waikato, in Hamilton. It’s not about bringing everything back to Wellington, like we’ve been talking about; it’s actually about it being out in the regions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of fact that Te Pūkenga's head office was located in Hamilton, in the Waikato, rather than in Wellington.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's annual reports and Crown entity registration records for its registered/head office address: true if the head office is recorded in Hamilton, Waikato; false if recorded in Wellington or elsewhere.

veracity.statement: In fact, they’ve been bailed out twice by the Government over the last 20 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Western Institute of Technology at Taranaki (WITT) received two separate government financial rescues in roughly the two decades before 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and Ministry of Education records of exceptional financial assistance, Crown loans or capital injections to WITT since about 2005, plus WITT's annual reports: true if two or more such interventions are recorded; false if fewer.

veracity.statement: As Chris Penk has previously stated in the House, it is around 50 percent more expensive to build a stand-alone house in New Zealand than in Australia.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Chris Penk that the cost of constructing a stand-alone house in New Zealand is approximately 50 percent higher than in Australia.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Trans-Tasman residential construction cost comparisons (NZ Infrastructure Commission / former Productivity Commission housing affordability work, MBIE build-cost analysis, or Rider Levett Bucknall / CoreLogic cost indices) for stand-alone dwellings: true if New Zealand per-square-metre or per-dwelling build costs are around 50 percent above the Australian equivalent; false if the gap is materially smaller or reversed.

rigor.statement: Well, I’m assuming most of the members know that the head office for Te Pūkenga actually is in the Waikato, in Hamilton. It’s not about bringing everything back to Wellington, like we’ve been talking about; it’s actually about it being out in the regions.
rigor.explanation: The premise supports only the narrow point that the head office was not in Wellington. The conclusion drawn — that the model was 'about it being out in the regions' — does not follow: a single head office in Hamilton is still centralisation, just not Wellington-based. Non sequitur between the geographic fact and the claim about the model's character.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But we didn’t really hear from homeowners, because they are not resourced to give those kinds of submissions in the select committee process, and so we will not know how this has a long-term impact on not only consumers and household owners who are affected by this but also for their insurance and for their banks.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: limited submitter capacity among homeowners is offered as the reason the long-term consumer, insurance and lending effects are unknown. The premise supports some evidentiary gap, but the conclusion that we 'will not know' the long-term impact overreaches what unheard submissions could have supplied — a gap between what was shown and what was concluded, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You know, it’s not unnecessary paperwork; it’s just something to help them be able to get lending from a bank, insurance from an insurer, keep their costs down, and make sure they can live in the building safely.
rigor.explanation: Argues that Building Act compliance documentation is not red tape, and supports the conclusion with the concrete downstream uses of that documentation — bank lending, insurance, cost, safety. The reasons offered genuinely bear on the conclusion; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We think that there will be 13,000 more dwellings because of this legislation, and that is a good thing.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a specific future outcome attributable to the bill: 13,000 additional dwellings resulting from the new small-dwelling regime. Not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Stats NZ building consent and exemption data for small stand-alone dwellings built under this Act's regime, measured against the counterfactual baseline in the bill's regulatory impact statement over the period that estimate covers (10 years from commencement); true if cumulative additional dwellings reach approximately 13,000, false if materially fewer.

specificity.statement: We think that there will be 13,000 more dwellings because of this legislation, and that is a good thing.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete, checkable figure (13,000 dwellings) tied to a named piece of legislation, but supplies no timeframe, distribution or mechanism for how the number arises.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: You know, we’ve seen 20,000 jobs in building and construction gone since the day of the election.
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable figure anchored to a named sector and a named starting point (the election). Someone could look this up directly; it lacks only the source series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are supporting this because housing is critically important to people, and anything that will bring down the cost of housing is something we will be working hard to find the merit in, and this is one of those.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the substantive reason for the party's position but carries no figure, mechanism or threshold — 'housing is critically important' and 'anything that will bring down the cost' commit to nothing checkable, and no nearby sentence supplies the detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You know, we’ve seen 20,000 jobs in building and construction gone since the day of the election.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that employment in the building and construction sector has fallen by 20,000 between the 2023 general election and the date of the speech (October 2025). Asserted by the speaker in her own voice, not relayed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / Household Labour Force Survey employment for the construction industry, comparing October 2023 with the most recent quarter before October 2025; true if the fall is approximately 20,000, false if materially smaller or if employment rose.

veracity.statement: We’re also seeing more and more young New Zealanders who could be taking up those opportunities and building apprenticeships and getting into building, from whatever walk of life they are from, either leaving our shores—200 young New Zealanders a day—or not able to get into those jobs in building and construction.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current departure rate of 200 young New Zealanders per day (roughly 73,000 a year) leaving the country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for New Zealand citizen departures in the year to the date of the statement, restricted to the younger age bands the claim refers to (broadly under 30); true if that subset averages about 200 a day, false if the 200-a-day figure only holds for citizen departures of all ages combined or is materially lower.

focus.statement: There is a real question now, with the Government’s introduction of policy around how young people, particularly 18- and 19-year-olds, will be able to realise those supports, about what supports the building and construction sector will have when it needs to rapidly up its workforce and get more and more young New Zealanders into those jobs, unless we have rapid change in the immigration settings, that see more offshore builders being able to come in to fill those.
focus.explanation: Names a specific government policy (the changes affecting 18- and 19-year-olds' access to support) and a specific policy lever (immigration settings), and connects both to the workforce the bill depends on. This is scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is a real question now, with the Government’s introduction of policy around how young people, particularly 18- and 19-year-olds, will be able to realise those supports, about what supports the building and construction sector will have when it needs to rapidly up its workforce and get more and more young New Zealanders into those jobs, unless we have rapid change in the immigration settings, that see more offshore builders being able to come in to fill those.
civility.explanation: Contested ground — she is criticising a government policy on a bill she opposes in part — and the criticism lands entirely on the policy and its consequences. No person is characterised or impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That’s really important, and I’d say that this Government has kind of done the opposite, really, by cancelling a bunch of State homes that would have been built over the last few years that would have helped address the housing shortage but also would have kept builders and construction companies employed during this time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Government cancelled State (public) house builds that had been planned for the preceding few years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora build programme records and Budget 2024/2025 documents on planned public housing places: true if a material number of previously committed/planned state house builds were cancelled or removed from the programme after October 2023; false if the programme was maintained or expanded with no cancellations.

veracity.statement: That cost councils a fortune, and that was the outcome of the last time the Government decided to massively deregulate the building sector in order to, supposedly, achieve productivity, make it cheaper, make it easier to build more homes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two linked facts: that the leaky-buildings crisis imposed large costs on local councils, and that it followed a previous deregulation of the building sector undertaken in the name of productivity and cheaper building.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hunn Report (2002), the Weathertight Homes Resolution Service / Financial Assistance Package records, and PwC's cost estimates for the leaky homes crisis: true if councils carried a substantial share of remediation cost (e.g. the 25% council share under the FAP, plus litigation settlements) and if official inquiries attribute the failure in part to the deregulatory 1991 Building Act regime; false if councils bore negligible cost or if the inquiries attribute the crisis to unrelated causes.

veracity.statement: From the regulatory impact statement, it’s estimating approximately 7,800 additional granny flats—maybe the numbers are up a little bit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement accompanying the bill estimates roughly 7,800 additional small standalone dwellings, in contrast to the 13,000 figure cited by the previous speaker.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE regulatory impact statement for the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill: true if its central estimate of additional dwellings is approximately 7,800; false if the estimate is materially different (e.g. 13,000).

divination.statement: Our building code is, actually, wholly insufficient, and we will be facing another issue of something similar to the leaky buildings over the next 10 or 20 years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that a systemic building-defect problem comparable in kind to the leaky-buildings crisis will emerge within 10–20 years, attributed to deficiencies in the current building code.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE / Building Officials or weathertightness-style inquiry reporting by 2045: true if a systemic, sector-wide defect problem (e.g. widespread structural or mould/moisture failure in dwellings built under the current code) is officially identified on a scale drawing comparison with the leaky homes crisis; false if no such systemic failure is identified by that date.
