focus.statement: The bill implements the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State and Faith-Based Care to, firstly, recognise the experience as a person of abuse in care, and, secondly, to offer an alternative to litigation to be able to provide that redress.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the measure before the House does — its source, its two stated purposes and the litigation alternative. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What’s being proposed here—and this is particularly for Minister Costello, who seems to be saying something quite different—is a presumption, a presumption that people in this situation have no right to redress.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of the bill — a presumption against redress for a defined class — and disputes the responsible Minister's characterisation of it. The reference to the Minister is about what she has said on the measure, not about the other team in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It has been quite annoying, actually, to sit over here on this side and listen to some of the claims that have been coming from across the House, because I think that there will be abuse survivors who are listening at home and some of them may actually be upset to hear the claims from the other side—which are untrue—that this is going to mean that some people aren’t going to be able to get access to redress.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point — what the bill does to redress access — but it is carried inside a complaint about what "the other side" is saying and how it feels to listen to them. A real policy claim wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: My mother, I think I've said before, spent 20 years, the longest serving Parole Board member in this country, appointed by the National Government—appointed by the Rt Hon Jim Bolger, actually, who we're going to honour on Thursday.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts about June Jackson: a 20-year tenure on the Parole Board, that this made her the longest-serving member in New Zealand, and that she was appointed under Jim Bolger's National Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Parole Board membership and appointment records (and contemporaneous reporting of her appointment/retirement); true if her service ran approximately 20 years, was the longest of any board member, and began under a Bolger-era National appointment; false if the tenure is materially shorter, another member served longer, or the appointing government was different.

veracity.statement: What’s more, the royal commission recommended that survivors who are in prison or have a criminal record should not be unduly penalised—clear as a bell—but, sadly, this bill penalises those people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care explicitly recommended that survivors who are in prison or have criminal records should not be unduly penalised in redress.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's final report (Whanaketia) and its redress recommendations; true if a recommendation states that a survivor's imprisonment or criminal record should not bar or reduce redress, false if no such recommendation appears or the report leaves the question open.

veracity.statement: They save about $12,500 if the person stands by the presumption, and that is inappropriate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Crown saves approximately $12,500 in each case where a claimant is subject to the bill's presumption against redress.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill's regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure statement and the average redress payment figures published for the scheme; true if the per-claimant saving implied by the presumption is approximately $12,500, false if the published figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Actually, this doesn’t apply to most people. Only 5 to 6 percent of claimants may even fall into this category, and most of them have not gone on to cause other victims in the system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified estimate — that only 5 to 6 percent of redress claimants fall within the category affected by the bill's exclusion, and that a majority of that group have not gone on to harm others.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Officials' advice on the bill (regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure statement) and MSD/Crown Response claimant data; true if the estimated share of claimants captured by the provision is in the 5–6% range and the offending-against-others share within that group is below half, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: It has been quite annoying, actually, to sit over here on this side and listen to some of the claims that have been coming from across the House, because I think that there will be abuse survivors who are listening at home and some of them may actually be upset to hear the claims from the other side—which are untrue—that this is going to mean that some people aren’t going to be able to get access to redress.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of fact that the Opposition's characterisation is untrue — that is, that no claimant will be denied access to redress under the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill as introduced, specifically the provisions governing claimants with serious convictions; true if every claimant retains an avenue to redress, false if the bill creates a presumption or bar that removes redress eligibility from any class of claimant.

divination.statement: So, obviously, you're going to get an angry response from many of the victims out there.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that abuse-in-care survivors will react angrily to the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill — an outcome about other people's reaction, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Select committee submissions on the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill and public statements by survivor groups/advocates; true if a substantial body of survivor submissions and survivor-group statements oppose or criticise the bill's exclusion provisions, false if survivor submissions are largely supportive or negligible in number.

specificity.statement: The bill implements the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State and Faith-Based Care to, firstly, recognise the experience as a person of abuse in care, and, secondly, to offer an alternative to litigation to be able to provide that redress.
specificity.explanation: Names the bill, the inquiry and two concrete purposes, but carries no figures, thresholds, timeframes or entitlement detail — a description of direction rather than of mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They save about $12,500 if the person stands by the presumption, and that is inappropriate.
specificity.explanation: A named dollar figure attached to a named mechanism (the presumption), checkable and actionable. Marked down slightly because the basis of the figure — per claimant, per claim, or in total — is left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Actually, this doesn’t apply to most people. Only 5 to 6 percent of claimants may even fall into this category, and most of them have not gone on to cause other victims in the system.
specificity.explanation: A precise percentage range tied to a defined population of claimants, plus a stated proportion within it. Someone could go and check it against the officials' advice.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My concern with this law is it will do the opposite. It shirks responsibility for cruel acts, for things that harmed people so, so absolutely deeply that it set their lives absolutely askew.
civility.explanation: Severe language — "shirks responsibility", "cruel acts" — but every word of it is aimed at the legislation, not at any member. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And we have not seen a great deal of action from this Government, so perhaps they have been distracted—unless you call kicking the can down the road “action”.
focus.explanation: There is a real accountability point underneath (the Government has not acted on the royal commission), but no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the weight of the sentence is a sarcastic characterisation of the other side. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The change to the Crimes Act to include disabled people as vulnerable adults was not supported by submitters. As a result, if passed, we will have something in legislation that is not supported by the people it is supposed to be there for.
focus.explanation: Names the specific amendment (the Crimes Act change on vulnerable adults) and the specific defect in it. Squarely on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Further, we were concerned about the inclusion of the potential use of force during searches at youth justice facilities, and I submitted several amendments to include the use of proven de-escalation methods as an approach to avoiding the use of force—but these were not supported by the Minister and the Government.
focus.explanation: Entirely about a specific provision of the bill and a specific amendment moved to it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In their response to the royal commission, published in May this year, the Government declined to accept, or had not even started to consider, 85 of the royal commission’s 207 recommendations from across the two reports, Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu. The Government has fully accepted only 19 recommendations, and they claim to have completed a mere 13.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four countable facts about the Crown's May 2025 response to the Abuse in Care Royal Commission: 207 recommendations in total across Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu; 85 declined or not yet considered; 19 fully accepted; 13 claimed complete.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown's published response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care (released May 2025) and its recommendation-tracking table: true if the totals match 207 recommendations, 85 declined/not started, 19 fully accepted and 13 reported complete (within rounding of category boundaries); false if the published tallies differ materially.

specificity.statement: In their response to the royal commission, published in May this year, the Government declined to accept, or had not even started to consider, 85 of the royal commission’s 207 recommendations from across the two reports, Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu. The Government has fully accepted only 19 recommendations, and they claim to have completed a mere 13.
specificity.explanation: Four exact counts, a named source document, a publication month and both named reports. Directly checkable against the Crown response.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Further, we were concerned about the inclusion of the potential use of force during searches at youth justice facilities, and I submitted several amendments to include the use of proven de-escalation methods as an approach to avoiding the use of force—but these were not supported by the Minister and the Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the provision (use of force during searches at youth justice facilities), the concrete alternative proposed (de-escalation methods via amendments) and the outcome. Missing only the amendment numbers and the detail of the methods.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We wholeheartedly welcome the removal of the use of strip searching for children and young people.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete, checkable change (removal of strip searching) and who it applies to, but carries no mechanism, timeframe or figures beyond the named measure.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The change to the Crimes Act to include disabled people as vulnerable adults was not supported by submitters. As a result, if passed, we will have something in legislation that is not supported by the people it is supposed to be there for.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure, but it slides from 'submitters' to 'the people it is supposed to be there for' — a hasty generalisation treating those who made submissions as representative of all disabled people. The conclusion follows only if that equation holds, and nothing is offered to support it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This Government’s approach to Māori, Pacific, disabled people, people receiving income support, and young people in the youth justice system demonstrates that discrimination is alive and well in this country.
rigor.explanation: Asserts that an unspecified 'approach' demonstrates a broad conclusion about discrimination, without offering a single policy, decision or datum as the premise. The word 'demonstrates' claims an entailment where nothing has been shown — a bare assertion presented as a derived conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister was well-placed to consult properly or to remove this part of the bill, or to do further consultation, but she chose not to. That goes against the entire point of the royal commission.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal in direction — it attributes a deliberate choice to the Minister and calls it contrary to the royal commission's purpose — but it stays on the decision rather than on her character, competence or motives. Robust criticism edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This sits alongside the Government’s pilot boot camp legislation, to put these into law—no doubt soon—to be again considered in this House.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government's pilot boot camp (military-style academies) legislation will return to the House and be enacted in the near future. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — it predicts the Government's bill completing its passage.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bills register for the Government bill establishing military-style academies / boot camps for young offenders: true if it has its remaining stages and receives royal assent by the resolve-by date, false if it is still before the House, withdrawn, or defeated at that date.

specificity.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact inserted provision (new section 384KB) and the clause that inserts it (clause 28), and identifies the substantive issue (permitted use of force in care settings). Someone could go to the bill text and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So it is important that we note and continue to work with those concerns and that instead there must be—and this is hard but enduring—co-design approaches, proper relationship engagement design approaches to legislative protections for and with the disability community to ensure that the language does not continue to rob them of their dignity and mana.
specificity.explanation: Names a method (co-design) and the community it should involve, which is more than a slogan, but supplies no mechanism, no process, no timeframe and no proposed wording change. 'Proper relationship engagement design approaches' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures against a named body of recommendations — directly checkable against the Crown response reporting. The 'move a heck of a lot faster' half is vague, but the claim carrying the weight is exact.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That continues to normalise violence. It moves us away instead from the de-escalation techniques and the violence prevention techniques that we instead should be prioritising.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy provision: permitting use of force normalises violence and displaces de-escalation practice. But the causal step is asserted rather than supported — nothing is offered to connect a statutory permission to normalisation, and the claim that it 'moves us away' from de-escalation assumes the two are mutually exclusive. A genuine gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So there is concern that the changes contribute to further and re-institutionalising youth justice residences when, again, instead there should be a shift away from the punitive, institutionalised models and towards community-based and trauma-informed care models.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the bill does — its effect on youth justice residences — and names the alternative model being argued for. No party framing at all; this is engagement with the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has that bench seen this times nine [Holds up report] of the reports and the evidence and the harm and the lived experience of survivors to then stand up and demand us to not be emotive? What is that bench saying about the level of recognition that violence deserves?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's conduct in the debate — how long they spoke, what they demanded of her, what their attitude reveals. No policy, clause, figure or outcome is named in it. The one concrete referent is the stack of reports she holds up, which is not a policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
focus.explanation: A third reading of a named bill is before the House, so there is ample policy to engage with, but this engages none of it. It is purely a characterisation of what the other side said and how it was said.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures about implementation of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's recommendations: that the final report made 138 recommendations, and that as at October 2025 only 28 of them had been completed or had progress initiated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, June 2024) recommendation count, and the Crown Response Office's published progress reporting on those recommendations as at October 2025. True if the report contains 138 recommendations and roughly 28 are recorded as completed or with progress initiated; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: That we are ensuring that our responses are culturally grounded, recognising that the majority of survivors are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori make up the majority — i.e. more than half — of survivors of abuse in State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia) estimates of the ethnic composition of survivors of abuse in State and faith-based care. True if Māori are estimated at more than 50% of survivors over the inquiry period; false if the estimate is below 50% (disproportionate representation relative to population share would not on its own make the claim true).

civility.statement: Has that bench seen this times nine [Holds up report] of the reports and the evidence and the harm and the lived experience of survivors to then stand up and demand us to not be emotive? What is that bench saying about the level of recognition that violence deserves?
civility.explanation: Aimed at the opposite benches collectively rather than at any individual, so it is not a personal insult — but it imputes bad faith and indifference to survivors' harm ('what is that bench saying about the level of recognition that violence deserves'). That is sneering at motive rather than engaging the argument, which is a real failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the previous speech as 'rubbish' that has been 'spouted' — contemptuous of the speaker rather than of the argument, and it engages nothing in it. Directed at the other side as a bloc rather than at Davidson by name, which keeps it short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yeah, well, I’m actually one of those survivors, so can you just calm it down and allow people to have their own opinions without rubbishing everybody under one category, because at the end of the day, we can talk to multiple survivors who will all have a different version of how this has affected them, how this has traumatised them, and how they want us, as a Government, to respond to that.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personally directed — 'can you just calm it down' and the accusation of 'rubbishing everybody' address the interjector's conduct rather than only the argument — but it lands no insult and moves quickly onto the substantive point about survivors differing. Robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Reasonable force is not about violence; reasonable force is done in good practice, with good training, to make sure that de-escalation does happen first, before reasonable force is used, and to say that that’s not going to happen is actually disingenuous.
civility.explanation: 'Disingenuous' imputes bad faith to those making the criticism — it says they know better and are arguing dishonestly. Short of a direct insult, but under the re-anchored scale that is a genuine civility failure rather than merely robust debate.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In the committee of the whole House, it was explained quite well to the Opposition that de-escalation training will happen, and so to say that that was not addressed is actually quite a joke—to say that we didn’t address that problem.
civility.explanation: 'Quite a joke' is mockery of the opposing case rather than engagement with it — it dismisses the criticism as ridiculous instead of answering why the committee explanation should settle it. Sneering falls at the failure point of the scale.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has worked tirelessly in the background, changing practice across the youth justice system and professionalising the youth justice system to make sure that our young people are actually cared for in a way that is appropriate.
specificity.explanation: Names a domain (youth justice practice) but supplies no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named programme — 'changing practice' and 'professionalising' are directional claims of activity that nobody could check or act on. Not a pure slogan, so above the floor.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the Oranga Tamariki Act, the changes are around clarifying secure care, which was really quite a muddy ground. Young people didn’t actually have the security of knowing how long they were going to be in secure care, and so we are changing that.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute (Oranga Tamariki Act), the provision area (secure care) and the specific defect being fixed (duration not knowable). Missing the actual mechanism — what the new limit or notification requirement is — and any timeframe, so it sits mid-scale rather than at the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On top of the changes to the Public Records Act there is work going on in the background—particularly with Oranga Tamariki—around an upgrade to our front-line technology system, which will allow young people to have access to their lives in their own time and under their own rules on how they want to be able to access their information.
specificity.explanation: Names a statute (Public Records Act), an agency (Oranga Tamariki) and a concrete deliverable (a front-line technology system upgrade giving care-experienced people self-service access to their records). No cost, no delivery date and no description of what the system actually is, so it stops short of checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill is a start. The bill is a process. Change needed to happen; more change will continue to need to happen.
specificity.explanation: Four clauses that commit to nothing checkable — no provision, no figure, no timeframe, and no indication of what the further change would be. 'More change will continue to need to happen' is a placeholder for content rather than content.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Reasonable force is not about violence; reasonable force is done in good practice, with good training, to make sure that de-escalation does happen first, before reasonable force is used, and to say that that’s not going to happen is actually disingenuous.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure before the House, and a weak one: it defines reasonable force by its intended best practice ('good practice', 'good training', de-escalation first) and concludes it will not be violent, which assumes the compliance that critics are disputing. Question-begging — the design intent is offered as evidence that the outcome will match it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think that to say that there was no consultation is a little bit low, because there was six years of consultation.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation on 'consultation'. The criticism is that survivors were not consulted on the contents of this bill; the rebuttal substitutes the six years of Royal Commission inquiry consultation, which was about the abuse itself, not about the drafting of these amendments. The conclusion does not follow because the two senses of the term are not the same thing.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is a difficult process to pass legislation, so that is why it has taken longer than I think many of us would have wanted it to.
rigor.explanation: A premise-and-conclusion pair, but the premise is generic: legislating is difficult in general, which is true of every bill and so cannot explain why this particular one was slower than hoped. Nothing specific to this bill's passage is offered to connect the two, leaving a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the committee of the whole House, it was explained quite well to the Opposition that de-escalation training will happen, and so to say that that was not addressed is actually quite a joke—to say that we didn’t address that problem.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that during the committee of the whole House stage on this bill, the Government explained to Opposition members that de-escalation training would accompany the reasonable-force provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the committee of the whole House stage on the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill: true if a Minister or Government member there stated that de-escalation training would be provided before or alongside the use of reasonable force; false if no such exchange appears in that stage's record.

veracity.statement: Look, we hear it quite a bit that these changes that are done have not been done in consultation with survivors, but what I would say is that there was six years of consultation with survivors: six years of an inquiry into the abuse in care, six years of listening to survivors, and six years of writing survivors’ stories, to be held and written for everybody to be able to read that going into the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care ran for six years and that its work consisted of hearing from and recording the accounts of survivors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care in State and Faith-based Institutions: its date of establishment by Order in Council and the date of its final report, plus its published count of survivor engagements. True if the elapsed span is approximately six years (±1) and survivor testimony was a documented core activity; false if the inquiry ran materially shorter or longer, or did not take survivor accounts.

veracity.statement: The previous Government knew that this inquiry was happening, it knew of some of the recommendations well before we came into Government, and I think that we need to stop attacking each other and actually work together to move forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous (Labour-led) Government was aware of the abuse-in-care inquiry and had received at least some of its recommendations before the change of government in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The publication dates of the Royal Commission's interim reports and their recommendations against the date of the 2023 change of government (October 2023). True if one or more reports containing recommendations were delivered to the previous Government before that date; false if all recommendations post-date the change of government.

veracity.statement: At no point has the Government or anyone debating this issue in the House suggested this is an end point.
veracity.explanation: A universal claim about what was said in the House: that no Government member, and indeed no participant in the debate on this bill, characterised the legislation as the complete or final response to the royal commission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of all stages of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill. False if any member speaking on the bill described it as the end point, the completion of the response, or otherwise as sufficient in itself; true if every speaker who addressed the point framed it as a first step or partial response.

focus.statement: Whilst I appreciate that the Opposition is supporting these bills, what I would have appreciated more would be their speaking to the positive changes and speaking about how this will have a great effect on those who have fought for years to be heard and who have fought for years to have some of these changes made—and it was all made political.
focus.explanation: Strip out the characterisation of how the Opposition chose to debate and nothing about the measure remains — no clause, figure, mechanism or outcome is named. It is a complaint about the other side's tone and motives ('it was all made political'), not about the policy. No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly; this is the tribal framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I refuse to hear from those in this House that think we are not allowed to be emotional about any part of this bill.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the conclusion rests on a position attributed to other members — that emotion is not allowed — which no one in the debate has advanced (Joseph Mooney interjects "Never said that"). The premises about the House's emotional response support only that emotion was present, not that anyone claimed it was disallowed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Colonisation is political, and to deny that in this House is to deny the very existence of the pain and the reason why they were in State care.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy. Disputing that a matter is political does not entail denying that the harm occurred; the two claims are treated as one, with nothing offered to connect them.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are, unfortunately, many cases where people will use force against themselves or others, and reasonable force needs to be used to stop that, so let's have a responsible conversation as we continue this piece of work, ladies and gentlemen.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote, generalised across a change of setting: the single incident offered involved an adult prisoner assaulting a lawyer in a corrections facility, while the provision at issue concerns force used on young people in Oranga Tamariki care. The conclusion that the provision is justified does not follow from the example given.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our solutions that we had were there, right in front of us all, to agree across every party in this House, and that was to adopt the 138 recommendations of the Whanaketia report—138 recommendations.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific report and the exact count of recommendations being called for — a concrete, actionable alternative to the bill rather than a general call for change. Falls short of 1.0 only because it does not say which recommendations matter most or by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They wanted to ban strip-searches of children, stop the treating of trauma with trauma.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete, checkable practice to be prohibited, though it gives no mechanism, threshold or timeframe for the ban.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The research found that one-in-five within our prison system has been a victim of abuse in State care.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete proportion attached to a defined population, so it can be checked. Marked down because the research is not named, leaving the reader to identify the source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are some changes to be made to the Oranga Tamariki Act, the Children's Act, the Crimes Act, and the Public Records Act—an omnibus bill, to make some changes to that.
specificity.explanation: Names the four statutes the bill amends, which is checkable, but gives no figures, mechanisms or timeframes for what the amendments actually do.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our solutions that we had were there, right in front of us all, to agree across every party in this House, and that was to adopt the 138 recommendations of the Whanaketia report—138 recommendations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's Whanaketia report contains 138 recommendations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, Whanaketia – Through pain and trauma, from darkness to light (July 2024); true if the report sets out 138 recommendations, false if it contains a materially different number.

veracity.statement: They asked for the disestablishment of Oranga Tamariki.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the survivors, or the inquiry recording their evidence, sought the disestablishment of Oranga Tamariki as an agency — not merely its reform.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whanaketia report's recommendations and the survivor evidence and submissions it records; true if disestablishment (abolition) of Oranga Tamariki was among what survivors asked for, false if what was sought was reform, oversight or transfer of functions while the agency continued to exist.

veracity.statement: The research found that one-in-five within our prison system has been a victim of abuse in State care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research establishes that approximately 20 percent of the New Zealand prison population were abused while in State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Whanaketia report and the Department of Corrections / Royal Commission research it cites on the proportion of prisoners with a history of abuse in State care; true if the published figure is about one in five, false if the published figure is materially different (e.g. nearer one in three, or nearer one in ten).

veracity.statement: There are some changes to be made to the Oranga Tamariki Act, the Children's Act, the Crimes Act, and the Public Records Act—an omnibus bill, to make some changes to that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill amends these four specific Acts: the Oranga Tamariki Act, the Children's Act, the Crimes Act and the Public Records Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill as passed at third reading; true if all four named Acts appear among the enactments it amends, false if any of the four is not amended by the bill.

focus.statement: They wanted to ban strip-searches of children, stop the treating of trauma with trauma.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure the speaker says the bill omits — a prohibition on strip-searching children in care. Squarely on the content of the legislation, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is incremental change, and we believe it is not moving fast enough to bring about some reconciliation for those who have been harmed at the hands of the Crown by those who were meant to look after them.
focus.explanation: Directed at the legislation itself and its rate of progress rather than at the other party, but it names no particular provision, recommendation or outcome, so it sits below the accountability standard set by a named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are, unfortunately, many cases where people will use force against themselves or others, and reasonable force needs to be used to stop that, so let's have a responsible conversation as we continue this piece of work, ladies and gentlemen.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual measure at issue — the de-escalation and reasonable-force amendments to the Oranga Tamariki Act — rather than the Opposition's character. On-policy, notwithstanding the weakness of the supporting inference.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I think the sad thing is that if we had a Prime Minister who truly supported this apology, then he would have proved it, and this Government would have proved it in everything they did.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Prime Minister personally — that his apology was not sincerely meant — rather than criticising the adequacy of the bill. Short of a direct insult, but it turns on the person's honesty rather than the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is incremental change, and we believe it is not moving fast enough to bring about some reconciliation for those who have been harmed at the hands of the Crown by those who were meant to look after them.
civility.explanation: A direct criticism of the Government's pace of reform in a genuinely contested third-reading debate, made without any imputation against a person. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unfortunately, some members of this House are very aware of that, and they are seeking to use this for political gain, which is unfortunate because this is a serious issue and a serious matter for many, many New Zealanders, both those directly affected, those indirectly affected, and for all of us.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to named-by-implication members — that they are exploiting survivors' suffering for advantage — rather than engaging what they actually argued. Not a direct insult, but it attributes a dishonourable motive to persons.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, I'm going to share one little story to say why these people should really wake up and live in the real world: a number of years ago, I was working as a lawyer, and I was contacted by a father of a young man who'd been accused of a very serious crime.
civility.explanation: "These people should really wake up and live in the real world" is condescension aimed at other members rather than at their argument — it characterises opponents as naive instead of addressing what they said about the use-of-force provisions.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve got a situation where children are going through strip-searches, and they’re going through a process of going into an environment which is not ideal, to say the least. We have come to an agreement, in this legislation, that that won’t happen anymore, and that was a really good thing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names a specific practice (strip-searching of children in care) and the specific change the legislation makes to it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s an incredibly important thing, because we know this is a place where violence grows—a relationship where somebody has no choice but to be there is a place where violence grows and there is predatory behaviour—so it’s really important that we make these amendments, and we change the system so that we’re checking overseas convictions.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: premise that custodial relationships where the person cannot leave are where predatory behaviour develops, conclusion that background vetting including overseas convictions should be strengthened. The conclusion tracks the premise; the gap is that nothing is offered connecting overseas convictions specifically to that risk mechanism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One is that pharmacists and nurse practitioners will have their ability to prescribe medications expanded. That is particularly important in rural locations where nurse practitioners may be acting alone in remote areas and people need their prescriptions quickly.
rigor.explanation: Claim offered with a supporting reason: if nurse practitioners are the sole clinician in remote areas and prescriptions are needed promptly, expanded prescribing rights follow as a remedy. The inference holds; it stops short of 1.0 because no evidence is offered that prescribing delay is in fact the binding constraint in those locations.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’ve got way too high levels of domestic violence and sexual violence in this country, and sexual violence is actually on the rise.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that sexual violence in New Zealand is currently increasing — a claim about a trend in the present, distinct from the value judgement that levels are 'too high'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey (Ministry of Justice) sexual assault incidence/prevalence estimates and NZ Police recorded sexual assault and related offence counts for the years up to 2025. True if either series shows an increase beyond sampling error over the preceding years; false if the series are flat or declining.

veracity.statement: As a result of that, all three coalition parties campaigned on a concept, similar to what is in this bill, known as the rule of two.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National, ACT and New Zealand First each campaigned at the last election on a policy of the 'rule of two' type — automatic acceptance of medicines already consented in other jurisdictions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 general election health policy documents and manifestos of National, ACT and New Zealand First, plus their published campaign releases on medicines approval. True if all three contain a commitment to accept overseas regulatory approvals (two or more jurisdictions) as a route to New Zealand availability; false if any one of the three carried no such commitment.

specificity.statement: It’s a definition of a vulnerable adult in the situation where a person is unable, by reason of those definitions—and that’s age, sickness, mental impairment, disability—to withdraw himself or herself because they are in the charge of another person.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual statutory test being debated — the enumerated grounds and the operative condition of being unable to withdraw from another's charge. Someone could go and check it against the Crimes Act. Short of 1.0 because she paraphrases the provision rather than citing the section.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It simply says that if two other jurisdictions have consented a medication for an indication, then it can be used in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: States the operative mechanism exactly — the threshold (two jurisdictions), the unit (a medication for a given indication) and the consequence (availability here). Concrete enough to check against the bill or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t accept what Minister Chhour said when she said, “We have been engaging for six or seven years.” That is just not good enough.
civility.explanation: A flat rejection of a Minister's position on a genuinely contested point, aimed at the adequacy of the engagement rather than at Chhour herself. Pointed and robust — 'just not good enough' edges toward the Minister — but it imputes no bad faith and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t come here to criticise or condemn any of the stories from the Government, from Minister Chhour.
civility.explanation: A contested third reading where he had every opportunity to attack the responsible Minister, and he explicitly declines to. Engages the substance without turning on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It was clear that the Government cared more about—well, they probably won’t respect this view—how they look to voters than acting on the promises to survivors.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that ministers are motivated by electoral appearance rather than obligations to survivors — and the parenthetical sneer that members opposite 'probably won't respect this view' pre-emptively attributes contempt to them. Short of a direct insult, but past the civil line.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, you are politicising it, because you’re not listening to what we’re saying.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named member — that he is playing politics and refusing to listen. No insult, but it attributes motive rather than engaging what was said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I’m trying to say, Mr Seymour, is that one of the calls from survivors was that the Treaty of Waitangi be respected and be part of this whole legislation, but Mr Seymour has got this weird sort of resentment to the Treaty and doesn’t understand that part of the Treaty process is that there is a special consultation process that has to be set up with Māori, that Mr Seymour disagrees with and refuses to be part of.
civility.explanation: Ascribes a 'weird sort of resentment' and a failure of comprehension to a named member — a characterisation of the person's disposition rather than of his stated position on Treaty clauses.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is important the Government does well with this kaupapa, but when you have initiatives, like boot camps, that were clearly recommended against by experts in the community—absolutely adamant that that type of a strategy was not going to, and does not, benefit people who’ve been through the system—totally ignored by the Government, it does not help.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (boot camps), the specific advice against it, and the specific failure (ignoring that advice). This is scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I mean, how can we legitimately be against abuse in State care while still—and this is the point—allowing the State to use force, you know?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the use-of-force provision in the bill before the House — the mechanism itself, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was clear that the Government cared more about—well, they probably won’t respect this view—how they look to voters than acting on the promises to survivors.
focus.explanation: About the other side's supposed motives rather than any named measure, figure or outcome. There is a policy backdrop (redress promises) but no policy content in the claim itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, you are politicising it, because you’re not listening to what we’re saying.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the conduct of the other side in the exchange. Strip out the accusation and no policy, measure or outcome remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to understand that you have to consult with communities much better.
focus.explanation: Vague, but squarely directed at the consultation process the bill sets up rather than at the other party. Low detail is Specificity's problem, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Clearly, for some people, redress will mean they will get something; redress for others will mean they get nothing, no matter what the abuse they suffered.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure before the House — who the redress scheme covers and who it leaves out. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is important the Government does well with this kaupapa, but when you have initiatives, like boot camps, that were clearly recommended against by experts in the community—absolutely adamant that that type of a strategy was not going to, and does not, benefit people who’ve been through the system—totally ignored by the Government, it does not help.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that experts in the community clearly and adamantly advised against boot camps as a strategy for people who have been through the State care system, and that the Government ignored that advice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official advice and expert submissions on the military-style academies / boot camps pilot — Oranga Tamariki departmental advice to Ministers, the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care report, and submissions from care-experienced advocacy groups. True if expert advice recorded there recommended against boot camps for care-experienced young people and was not adopted; false if the advice was supportive or mixed, or if the Government adopted it.

veracity.statement: The former Minister Kelvin Davis went down the track of recommendations in terms of having an all-Maori board to respond to the types of tragedies that were was happening within the Oranga Tamariki system, where babies were being taken, and whānau were not being consulted.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kelvin Davis, as Minister, acted on recommendations by appointing an all-Māori board to Oranga Tamariki in response to uplifts of babies without whānau consultation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial appointment records and Oranga Tamariki annual reports for the board appointed under Kelvin Davis as Minister for Children (2020–2023). True if the board he appointed was composed entirely of Māori members; false if it included non-Māori members or if no such board was constituted on his recommendation.

veracity.statement: Just today—just today—in The Post, he criticises the manner in which the Government has gone about this process by limiting the involvement by survivors and by ignoring the call for a real, independent redress system.
veracity.explanation: Relays a published criticism: that Reweti Peters, in The Post that day, faulted the Government for restricting survivor participation in the process and for rejecting calls for an independent redress system.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Post (thepost.co.nz), articles published on or about 21 October 2025 carrying comment from Ihorangi Reweti Peters. True if such an item exists and he criticises the Government for limiting survivor involvement and for not establishing an independent redress system; false if no such item exists or its content differs materially.

veracity.statement: This is a legacy owed to the courageous nearly 2,400 survivors who provided their experience and shared their experience of abuse that has contributed to the commission’s work, which has now resulted in this additional step to improve the safety and wellbeing of children.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that close to 2,400 survivors contributed their accounts of abuse to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, July 2024) and its published participation statistics. True if the number of survivors who gave evidence or shared their experience with the inquiry is approximately 2,400 (say, 2,300–2,500); false if materially different.

rigor.statement: I mean, how can we legitimately be against abuse in State care while still—and this is the point—allowing the State to use force, you know?
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: the bill's stated purpose (ending abuse in care) is in tension with a provision permitting State use of force. But it treats sanctioned restraint and abuse as equivalent without offering anything to bridge them, and he immediately concedes 'some common sense is going to come into it', which undercuts the dichotomy he has just drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to understand that you have to consult with communities much better.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no mechanism, no threshold and no timeframe — 'much better' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Clearly, for some people, redress will mean they will get something; redress for others will mean they get nothing, no matter what the abuse they suffered.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a real distinction in the scheme's effect but names no eligibility criterion, category of survivor or clause, so nobody could check which group he means.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As other speakers have talked about, we are doing many things in the background.
specificity.explanation: 'Many things in the background' names no action, no agency, no amount and no date. Offered as substance, but there is nothing in it to check.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It doesn’t mean to say that people are going to walk away from the Government, and, as I said, others will be opposed to this bill today.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that parties other than Labour will vote against the bill at its third reading later the same sitting day.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, 21 October 2025. True if at least one party other than Labour voted against the bill; false if it passed with no party opposed.

civility.statement: There are such things as magnanimity and grace, but they take time to earn in the House, and some members clearly have not spent that much time here just yet, but we have hope for them, just as we have hope for all people.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at other members personally — suggesting they have not been in the House long enough to have earned grace, wrapped in mock charity ("we have hope for them"). No policy substance is engaged; the target is the members themselves, which is a genuine civility failure though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Allowing all prescribers to prescribe will mean that people can get access to medications at critical times.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — names the mechanism (extending prescribing rights) and the intended effect. No party framing or reference to opponents at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That means that there will be an estimated $90 million in economic benefit over the next decade from being able to have these conferences here.
specificity.explanation: Carries a figure ($90 million), a timeframe (the next decade) and a named cause (hosting medical conferences in New Zealand). Someone could go and check the underlying estimate.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That means that there will be an estimated $90 million in economic benefit over the next decade from being able to have these conferences here.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that permitting medical conferences at which unapproved/unfunded medicines can be marketed will generate roughly $90 million of economic benefit in New Zealand over the ten years following the change.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Regulation / MBIE regulatory impact and post-implementation material on the medical conferences amendment, plus conference-sector activity data for New Zealand 2026-2035. True if the cumulative economic benefit attributed to hosting these conferences over the decade is of the order of $90 million or more; false if the realised benefit is materially below that (e.g. under half), or if the conferences do not eventuate.

veracity.statement: This is something that has come through the Ministry for Regulation’s red tape tip line and is a very good example of the Government listening and responding so that there can be more opportunities for New Zealanders to do well and to have greater opportunity to improve their lives through their own efforts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about provenance: that the medical-conference change originated in a submission to the Ministry for Regulation's red tape tip line, rather than from another source.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Regulation reporting on the red tape tip line (published summaries of submissions and resulting actions) and the departmental/regulatory impact material for this Amendment Paper. True if the medicines-advertising / medical conference issue is recorded as a tip line submission that fed into this amendment; false if the change is documented as arising from another source (agency review, sector lobbying, Medsafe advice) with no tip line origin.

focus.statement: Yes, it may be a great idea; however, it has come through the Ministry for Regulation, which, we know, is a creation from the ACT Party and is an interesting institution given that it's supposed to be about deregulating but is actually also being seen as a bit of an institution for fast tracking.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — which agency originated the late amendment, and whether that agency's remit fits — but the weight of the sentence is the provenance of the Ministry for Regulation as an ACT Party creation rather than anything the amendment would do. A genuine point in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We were given no warning, as far as I'm aware, and I think it does show, again, a bit of a lack of respect for due process by this Government.
rigor.explanation: A premise (no notice of the amendment, so submitters could not be heard) supporting a conclusion (disregard for due process). The inference tracks the premise, though 'again' asserts a pattern that is not evidenced here, which is a modest gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is very difficult to get the economies of scale that are needed, and so, for that reason, we think it's a good idea to rationalise how we look at the safety and availability of medicines.
rigor.explanation: Premise (New Zealand is too small a market to achieve scale) offered in support of a conclusion (rationalise the medicines approval process). The inference follows, though the step from 'scale is hard' to 'this particular rationalisation is the answer' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We also are happy that the medicines that are introduced will still need a sponsoring pharmaceutical company. That does provide a level of accountability that, we feel, will avoid New Zealand becoming a dumping-ground for inferior batches of drugs or drugs that could potentially be harmful.
rigor.explanation: A mechanism (a required sponsoring company) is offered as the reason a risk is averted. The link from 'someone is accountable' to 'inferior batches will not arrive' is plausible but unsupported — a gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I certainly feel there are a lot of New Zealanders who would not want to see New Zealand emulate some of the jurisdictions such as the US, where watching dinner TV, every ad that comes on seems to be about some magic pill that is going to save your life or make you live to an old age.
rigor.explanation: The case against direct-to-consumer advertising rests on an assumed public preference ('a lot of New Zealanders would not want') plus an anecdotal impression of US television — an appeal to popularity resting on anecdote, with nothing offered to connect US advertising volume to a harm here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We see that strikes are coming up on 23 October, so clearly there are some issues within the health system.
rigor.explanation: Premise (imminent industrial action) offered in support of a conclusion (there are problems in the health system). The inference is sound as far as it goes, but 'clearly' overstates what a strike notice alone establishes about the system as a whole.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It does seem a little bit strange that when there's been other countries of the same ilk who have approved medicines that we would have to have a long, drawn-out procedure before they could be used here in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: An argument for recognising overseas approvals that rests on the intuition that duplication is 'strange'. Nothing is offered on why the comparator regulators' standards are equivalent, so the conclusion leans on an appeal to intuition rather than on evidence about the regulators.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And this is very important because we know, as COVID showed, sometimes there’s breaks in the supply chain. We need to have alternatives on hand because as I say, this is about the lives of New Zealanders and the quality of life of all New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: The first step is a real inference from a real example — supply chains broke during COVID, so alternatives are needed. The second leans on an appeal to emotion ('the lives of New Zealanders') in place of showing that widened prescribing rights are what closes that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We were given no warning, as far as I'm aware, and I think it does show, again, a bit of a lack of respect for due process by this Government.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism of the Government's handling of process. It imputes a lack of respect, which edges toward bad faith, but no individual is targeted and the complaint is about a concrete procedural act rather than anyone's character.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We also are happy that the medicines that are introduced will still need a sponsoring pharmaceutical company. That does provide a level of accountability that, we feel, will avoid New Zealand becoming a dumping-ground for inferior batches of drugs or drugs that could potentially be harmful.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete feature of the bill — the sponsoring-company requirement — and the risk it is meant to address, but supplies no figures, thresholds or description of how accountability would be enforced.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we are now looking at the Medicines Classification Committee being a ministerial appointment, we don't think that is correct. It should be appointed by the director-general.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific body, the specific provision objected to (appointment by the Minister), and the specific alternative sought (appointment by the director-general). Actionable as drafted.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In Kaitāia, there are some 3,000 whānau in Kaitāia that don’t have access to a GP right now.
specificity.explanation: A concrete figure tied to a named town and a named service gap. Checkable against enrolment data, even though 'whānau' rather than individuals leaves the unit slightly loose.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I think nearly 200 submitters came before the select committee in writing and orally, and there were about 30-odd in terms of oral submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the volume of submissions to the Health Committee on this bill: roughly 200 in total, of which roughly 30 were heard orally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Medicines Amendment Bill and the committee's published submissions list; true if total submissions received are close to 200 and oral submissions number around 30, false if either count is materially different.

veracity.statement: In Kaitāia, there are some 3,000 whānau in Kaitāia that don’t have access to a GP right now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 3,000 whānau in Kaitāia currently have no access to a general practitioner.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora primary care enrolment figures for the Kaitāia area as at late 2025, or the local PHO's reported unenrolled population; true if approximately 3,000 households or people are without an enrolled GP, false if the figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: We see that strikes are coming up on 23 October, so clearly there are some issues within the health system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of present fact that health-sector strike action was scheduled for 23 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Union strike notices (NZNO, ASMS or allied health unions) and news reporting for October 2025; true if health-sector industrial action was scheduled for 23 October 2025, false if no such strike was notified for that date.

specificity.statement: It will allow the medicines to be approved for distribution in New Zealand when they've been approved by two other overseas jurisdictions.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism of the bill (approval triggered by two overseas approvals) — concrete and checkable against the bill text, though no figures or dates attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those are the European Union, Australia, Canada, the United States of America, the United Kingdom, Singapore, and Switzerland.
specificity.explanation: An exhaustive named list of the recognised overseas regulators, attached to a stated 30-working-day timeframe. Fully checkable and directly usable by anyone trying to work out whether a given medicine qualifies.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They are extremely skilled, they are well trained—they have four years of training, they have 300 clinical hours—and they are good people to extend that part of the Act to.
specificity.explanation: Supplies concrete figures for the training standard (four years, 300 clinical hours) to support the prescribing extension, though the Act provision itself is not named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are a Government that puts patients first; therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: A slogan. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision — nothing anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We heard 185 submissions and oral evidence from 32 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the submission and oral-evidence counts received by the Health Committee on the Medicines Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Medicines Amendment Bill and the committee's published submissions list; true if 185 written submissions and 32 submitters heard in person, false if materially different counts.

veracity.statement: It doesn't include changes to existing drugs, new indications, formulations, or administration routes, and these actually make up a large share of the Medsafe applications.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the bill's new pathway is limited to new medicines, and that variations to existing medicines form a large share of Medsafe's application workload.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Medicines Amendment Bill as reported back (scope of the two-jurisdiction pathway), plus Medsafe's published application/approval statistics broken down by new medicine versus changed indication, formulation or route; true if the pathway excludes those categories and they exceed a substantial minority of applications, false if the pathway covers them or they are a small share.

veracity.statement: I find it is my obligation to remind the House that this Government is putting more money into health than ever before—ever before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that current health expenditure is at an all-time high. The claim is unqualified as to nominal versus real or per-capita terms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget appropriations for Vote Health across years; true if the current year's health appropriation exceeds every prior year in nominal terms, false if any earlier year was higher. Note whether the claim survives on a real (CPI-adjusted) or per-capita basis, since an unqualified 'more than ever' invites that reading.

veracity.statement: They are extremely skilled, they are well trained—they have four years of training, they have 300 clinical hours—and they are good people to extend that part of the Act to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the training requirements for the nurse practitioners and prescribers the bill would extend section 29 prescribing to: four years of training and 300 clinical hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nursing Council of New Zealand registered nurse prescriber / nurse practitioner scope-of-practice requirements; true if the required practicum is 300 clinical hours and the training pathway runs to about four years, false if the published requirements differ materially.

rigor.statement: Because they have really good clinical skill levels—very high clinical skill levels—enabling them to prescribe medicines under section 29 will ensure that if there is that break in the supply chain, as others have mentioned, these prescribers will be able to get these medicines out to patients.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: high clinical skill therefore safe to extend section 29 prescribing, therefore supply-chain breaks are bridged. The first step is asserted rather than shown, and 'will ensure' overstates what skill level alone guarantees — a gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Companies need to see a commercial reason to apply in the first place, and the biggest barrier to that is going to be and will remain Pharmac funding, not necessarily Medsafe approval times.
rigor.explanation: Identifies the binding constraint: approval speed cannot drive applications if the commercial incentive depends on funding. The conclusion follows from the premise about sponsor incentives; the ranking of barriers is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the only gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If a country has a medicine approved by two of those countries, then clearly it is appropriate for approval here.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is carried entirely by 'clearly'. Nothing is offered connecting two foreign approvals to appropriateness in the New Zealand context — an appeal to self-evidence in place of an argument about regulatory equivalence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We had a select committee process and if this amendment was something that was seen as beneficial and was on the boil, it would have been really good for the people who made submissions to be able to contribute their knowledge in this process.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from what she offers: the value of select committee scrutiny is expert and affected-party input, so an amendment arriving after that stage loses exactly that input. The Empire of Pain material is used as illustration of stakes rather than as the load-bearing premise, so it does not reduce to argument-by-anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We are a Government that puts patients first; therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: a self-description of the Government's intentions is offered as the reason to support the bill. Nothing about the bill's contents does any work in reaching the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Therefore, the outcome from that is that patients still won't benefit from those medications.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the faster approval pathway will not translate into patients actually receiving the medicines, because funding rather than approval is the binding constraint.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Medsafe records of medicines approved under the two-jurisdiction pathway cross-referenced with Pharmac funding decisions and dispensing data; false if a material number of medicines approved via the new pathway are funded and dispensed to New Zealand patients, true if approvals under the pathway do not translate into funded, dispensed medicines.

focus.statement: Technical appointments, we think, most definitely belong with the Director-General of Health and certainly not the Minister.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — names the specific provision (the Medicines Classification Committee appointment change) and states the alternative. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can't help but reflect on the fact that National’s focus on cutting corners, on shifting control to Ministers rather than making the system work for patients, has been a step in the wrong direction.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point inside it — ministerial control over appointments, which is the clause she opposes — but it is carried as a characterisation of what National as a party is like ('cutting corners'), so the weight of the sentence is party framing rather than the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's unfortunate that on something that has wide support of the House, the member who just resumed her seat, Tracey McLellan, couldn't but help herself to take the opportunity to spread misinformation about what this Government is doing in the health sector.
civility.explanation: Turns on the named member rather than her argument: 'couldn't but help herself' is condescension about her character, and 'spread misinformation' imputes bad faith rather than disputing a specific claim. Short of outright abuse, but well past pointed.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If the Minister has what sounds like a substantial amendment ready, I’d like to see it.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested point — she is criticising the Minister for producing an amendment outside the select committee process — and the criticism lands entirely on the process, with no imputation about the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Much like Miss White, I am disappointed that that hasn't been brought to the committee at an earlier stage, because, as I've said, I think this is an area of huge public interest, and I suspect that there would have been submissions in terms of what is and isn't permissible at those medical conferences.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested criticism of the Government's handling of the amendment, directed entirely at the process and timing rather than at any member. Pointed but attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill's regulatory impact statement sites research comparing the registration of medicines across 20 OECD countries, which, in shocking news, between 2011 and 2020, New Zealand ranked last for the approval of modern medicines.
specificity.explanation: Names a source (the bill's regulatory impact statement), a comparator set (20 OECD countries), a period (2011-2020) and a rank (last). Someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That was very painful, I’d have to say, as a GP, to have to prescribe medicines just because they were unavailable—that made it a section 29. It meant that otherwise approved medications, just because they came from a different manufacturer, were no longer able to be supplied, so it was very, very tedious.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual statutory mechanism at issue (a section 29 prescription) and the concrete trigger for it (an approved medicine sourced from a different manufacturer), but supplies no figures, volumes or timeframes for how often this bites.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This bill's regulatory impact statement sites research comparing the registration of medicines across 20 OECD countries, which, in shocking news, between 2011 and 2020, New Zealand ranked last for the approval of modern medicines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for the Medicines Amendment Bill cites research placing New Zealand last of 20 OECD countries for approval of modern medicines over 2011-2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement for the Medicines Amendment Bill and the study it cites (comparative registration timelines across 20 OECD countries, 2011-2020). True if the RIS cites such research and it ranks New Zealand last of 20 for approval of new/modern medicines in that window; false if the ranking, the country count or the period materially differ, or the RIS cites no such comparison.

veracity.statement: This is, of course, something that the Labour Government introduced and that, in July this year, was removed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that free prescriptions (removal of the $5 prescription co-payment) were introduced by the previous Labour Government and that the policy was reversed in July of the year the statement was made (July 2025).
veracity.subject: speaker
