specificity.explanation: Describes the bill entirely in generic terms — 'fit for purpose', 'better equip the relevant agencies' — with no offence, clause, agency, power or timeframe named. Nothing here could be checked or acted on, though a second-reading speech gave ample opportunity for detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It squarely criminalises covert, deceptive, corruptive, or coercive activity undertaken on behalf of a foreign power to harm New Zealand’s core interests, including national security, elections, and human rights.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual elements of the new offence — the conduct types (covert, deceptive, corruptive, coercive), the actor (on behalf of a foreign power), and the protected interests (national security, elections, human rights). A reader could match this against the bill text. Short of 1.0 only because no clause number or penalty is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Good national security law is precise, not broad; is balanced, not blunt.
specificity.explanation: A rhetorical couplet of paired virtues. No threshold, definition, safeguard or drafting test is named, so it commits to nothing checkable — the same sentence would fit any security bill in any Parliament.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The National Security Strategy, released in 2023, was right to identify foreign interference as a key and growing threat.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable facts about a named document: that New Zealand's National Security Strategy was released in 2023, and that it identifies foreign interference as a key and growing threat. The 'was right to' clause is her opinion; the underlying assertions of date and content are what is at issue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The publication record and text of New Zealand's National Security Strategy (DPMC). True if the strategy was published during calendar 2023 and names foreign interference among the principal or growing national security threats; false if it was published in a different year, or if foreign interference is absent from its identified threats.

veracity.statement: I’m appreciative of the of the 49 oral submitters and 705 submitters, in general, that expressed their concerns.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific counts for the select committee process on the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill: 49 submitters heard orally and 705 submissions in total.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report on the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill, which records the number of submissions received and the number of submitters heard. True if the report gives 705 submissions and 49 oral submitters (allowing for the committee's own stated tally); false if either figure differs materially.

rigor.statement: Laws designed to target foreign interference must be precisely defined and proportionately applied, ensuring they do not have a chilling effect on the legitimate political activity, advocacy, or even dissent, especially amongst diaspora communities who already face pressure from authoritarian regimes abroad.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: from the premise that diaspora communities already face external pressure, she concludes that broadly-drafted interference offences risk chilling their legitimate advocacy, and therefore must be tightly defined. The step from imprecise drafting to a chilling effect is asserted rather than evidenced — no mechanism or comparable case is offered — so there is a real gap, but the conclusion tracks the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve seen examples of this behaviour internationally, and we would be naive to assume Aotearoa is not immune to this.
rigor.explanation: Argues from overseas instances to New Zealand's own exposure — a legitimate inductive step, but nothing is offered to connect the overseas cases to conditions here, and the weight is carried by the word 'naive', which is a mild appeal to prudence rather than evidence. (The literal 'not immune' is a spoken word-order slip; the intended reading is plain from the surrounding sentences and is scored as intended.)
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: National security should never be an excuse for secrecy that excludes scrutiny.
civility.explanation: A pointed warning to the Government about how the powers may be used, aimed entirely at the practice of withholding scrutiny rather than at any Minister's character or motives. Robust criticism directed at conduct-in-the-abstract is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We want to continue to see this Government have a clear plan to resource and implement these capabilities effectively.
focus.explanation: Directed at the implementation of the measure before the House — resourcing and delivery of the capabilities the bill creates — rather than at the Government's general character or record. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy. Slightly short of 1.0 because no specific capability or funding line is identified, but vagueness is Specificity's concern, not this one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We still believe that that filing fee is too high and it will be prohibitive to those who want to pursue justice through the courts.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House — the filing fee set by the bill and its effect on access to the tribunal. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does Hipkins know you’re making an announcement?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal discipline — whether the member has her leader's authority. No policy, measure or figure is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: ACT in Government is about actually fixing what matters, and this is an important bill that adds to everything that the Government and ACT is doing to support our court system and ensure people actually have access to justice.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy referent (the bill, court access), but the weight of the sentence is party branding — a slogan about what ACT is 'about' rather than about the measure's mechanism or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We still believe that that filing fee is too high and it will be prohibitive to those who want to pursue justice through the courts.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (the filing fee) and the claimed effect, but supplies no figure, no threshold and no proposed alternative level — the $234/$468 numbers were available and not used.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The key aspect here is if you are making a claim that is $30,001 your filing fee will also be doubled in response to that, and whether we think that that is actually the right setting and whether other things could have been considered that phase in or proportionalise the filing fee.
specificity.explanation: Gives the exact boundary case ($30,001), the precise consequence (the fee doubles) and a named alternative mechanism (phasing or proportionalising the fee). Someone could act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are mechanisms under which the fees can be addressed through existing processes within the justice system.
specificity.explanation: The precise point in contention was whether any hardship waiver exists for the disputes tribunal fee; the answer names no regulation, no process and no eligibility test — 'mechanisms' and 'existing processes' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does Hipkins know you’re making an announcement?
civility.explanation: Sneering at the member personally, implying she is freelancing without authority, rather than engaging anything she said about the filing fee. Short of a direct insult but not civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I'm not going to listen to someone who is a tobacco lobbyist, frankly.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on another member's character and integrity in response to an interjection about relevance — imputes that she is bought rather than answering the point.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think it's worth noting that this is the third reading as we kind of went down a wrong track with the previous speaker.
civility.explanation: A pointed rebuke of the previous speaker's relevance, edging toward the person but stopping at his conduct in the debate rather than his character.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While people can now make a claim up to $60,000, there is no sort of, I guess, empirical evidence other than the assumption that we have seen throughout the committee stage that suggests there's any rationale behind the idea that people making claims above $30,000 naturally have nearly $500 that they're able to pay for this in the first place, which is one of the reasons why the Greens supported the Labour Party's amendment from the Hon Dr Duncan Webb in terms of having an opportunity to look at the hardship situations where the filing fee could be waived.
rigor.explanation: An argument from absence of evidence, but a defensible one: the officials' case rests on an assumption about applicants' cash on hand, and pointing out that the assumption is unevidenced puts the burden where it belongs. The gap is that it establishes only that the assumption is unproven, not that it is false — enough to support 'consider a waiver', not enough to support the stronger claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, the bill is very effective and will deliver exactly what it’s aiming to do, which is access to justice.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the premise offered — that unspecified fee mechanisms exist somewhere in the system — does not support the conclusion that the bill will 'deliver exactly' its aim. Nothing connects the existence of those mechanisms to applicants who cannot pay $468 up front, which was the objection being answered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But the District Court has that ability for hardship and for considerations and for waivers of that fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the District Court, unlike the disputes tribunal, has an existing mechanism to waive fees on hardship grounds.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: District Courts Fees Regulations 2009 and Ministry of Justice fee-waiver guidance: true if a registrar may waive, remit or postpone a District Court filing fee on financial-hardship grounds; false if no such provision exists.

veracity.statement: We’ve already seen an improvement in court timeliness, and I know Minister McKee is going to continue to work on that throughout this term because it is very important.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that court timeliness has already measurably improved under the current Government (a claim about the present/past; the second clause is a promise about his own side and is not part of this claim).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice published court timeliness statistics (median time to disposal and active caseload, District and High Court) comparing 2025 with 2023: true if the timeliness measures show improvement, false if they are unchanged or worse.

veracity.statement: There are mechanisms under which the fees can be addressed through existing processes within the justice system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that existing justice-system processes already allow the disputes tribunal filing fee to be addressed, which is offered as the rebuttal to the claim that no hardship waiver exists at the tribunal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Disputes Tribunals Act 1988, the Disputes Tribunals Rules 1989 and the associated fees regulations: true if there is an existing waiver, remission or postponement process for the tribunal filing fee available to an applicant in hardship; false if the only relief available is reimbursement or an order against the other party after a successful claim.

specificity.statement: The bill also amends the Disputes Tribunal Rules 1989 to introduce a new filing fee tier of $468 for claims of $30,001 or more to aid with cost recovery and reflect the higher private benefits of using the tribunal for higher value claims.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument amended, the exact fee ($468), the exact threshold ($30,001) and the rationale. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the justice space, we're focused on restoring law and order, but we're also focused on speeding up the wheels of justice so people can get on with their lives, get their disputes resolved, and continue prospering and doing well, like everybody aspires to do in this country.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general direction with no figures, mechanisms, named measures or timeframes — 'restoring law and order' and 'speeding up the wheels of justice' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We heard of some of these instances where a Master’s student was paid $9,000 for a full year’s work; she was owed $41,000 in total. But to bring her case to the tribunal, she had to forego more than a quarter of what she was owed.
specificity.explanation: A concrete submitted case with amounts ($9,000 paid, $41,000 owed) and a stated consequence that follows arithmetically from the $30,000 cap. Someone could check it against the committee's evidence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Access to justice is the cornerstone of a fair society, and Labour has always believed that justice should not depend on the size of your wallet or your ability to hire a lawyer.
specificity.explanation: A statement of principle carrying no figures, mechanism or commitment — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It's estimated that up to 2,000 claims a year could benefit from this process.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the future annual volume of claims in the $30,000-$60,000 band that will use the tribunal once the raised jurisdiction is in force.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal caseload statistics for the first full year after the raised jurisdiction takes effect; true if the number of claims filed with a value above $30,000 approaches ~2,000 a year, false if it is materially below (e.g. under half that).

rigor.statement: In essence, we've got quite a good, efficient system that works for smaller claims up to $30,000, and for a long time that figure hasn't been adjusted. There has been a lot of inflation and we think it makes sense to extend that boundary further to $60,000—a practical, pragmatic thing that will make a difference to the many hard-working New Zealanders who just want to get on with their lives and get their disputes resolved in a timely fashion.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the threshold has been eroded by inflation, therefore it should be raised. The conclusion broadly follows, but the specific figure is not tied to the premise — nothing offered connects cumulative inflation since the limit was set to a doubling of the cap rather than some other number.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Whilst the new fee tier might seem a barrier to justice, it's a very small portion of the potential value of the claim. Disputes Tribunal proceedings remain significantly cheaper than bringing proceedings to the District Courts where court and legal costs are incurred throughout the case.
rigor.explanation: Meets the objection with a proportionality argument and a comparison to the alternative forum, which is relevant. But there is a gap: 'small relative to the claim' does not answer affordability of an up-front cost, and the comparison is to a forum the affected claimants are said to be priced out of already, so the conclusion is only partly supported by what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Some have questioned whether increasing the tribunal’s cap will overburden it, but the evidence that we received is otherwise. The Ministry of Justice modelling shows that the system can absorb this change and that only a modest increase in the caseload is expected.
rigor.explanation: States the counterargument and answers it by citing the specific modelling put before the select committee. The conclusion tracks the evidence offered; the only weakness is that the modelling is asserted rather than described.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we believe it is not right that there should be a fees waiver for the District Court fee but no fees waiver for a disputes tribunal, which would be a lower form.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument: if the more expensive, more formal forum grants hardship relief, the cheaper accessible forum should at least match it. The inference is sound given the premise; it does not address whether the two fee regimes are funded on different bases.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Disputes Tribunal has one of the fastest disposal rates of all the courts and tribunals in New Zealand and is one of the busiest forums in the civil justice system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two comparative facts about current tribunal performance: that its case disposal rate ranks among the fastest of NZ courts and tribunals, and that its volume ranks among the highest in the civil justice system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court and tribunal statistics on median/mean time to disposal and annual case volumes; true if the Disputes Tribunal sits in the top group on both measures, false if other courts or tribunals clearly dispose of cases faster and carry more civil volume.

veracity.statement: Around 11,000 people each year use the tribunal to sort out their issues.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current annual number of users of the Disputes Tribunal is about 11,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal annual application/case statistics for recent years; true if the figure is around 11,000 a year (say within ~20%), false if it is materially different.

veracity.statement: There are legitimate reasons for a filing fee to cover the costs associated with a dispute resolution process; however, $468 is high to many New Zealanders right now—significantly higher than the $260 filing fees for the District Court and there is no associated fees waiver on the basis of hardship; there is such a waiver for the District Court.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable factual claims: that the District Court filing fee for an equivalent civil claim is $260, and that a hardship-based fee waiver exists for the District Court but not for the Disputes Tribunal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The District Court Fees Regulations and the Disputes Tribunal Rules 1989 as in force in October 2025; true if the District Court civil filing fee is $260 and its fee-waiver/hardship provision has no Disputes Tribunal counterpart, false if the fee differs materially or a hardship waiver exists for the tribunal.

veracity.statement: Sixty thousand exceeds the limit in which a no-asset insolvency is available.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $60,000 debt is above the maximum total debt for which the no asset procedure under NZ insolvency law can be used.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Insolvency Act 2006 no asset procedure eligibility threshold for total unsecured debt as at October 2025; true if that ceiling is below $60,000, false if it is $60,000 or more.

civility.statement: So we believe it is not right that there should be a fees waiver for the District Court fee but no fees waiver for a disputes tribunal, which would be a lower form.
civility.explanation: Directly contests a government drafting choice on a genuinely disputed point and does so entirely on the substance of the fee regime — no imputation of motive, no attack on the Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We feel that there has been a missed opportunity, that there have been a number of other improvements that could have been made to the Act.
focus.explanation: Criticism of the Government aimed squarely at the scope of the legislation before the House rather than at Labour's opponents in general; she goes on to name the specific gaps. No party framing or tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Let’s be very clear, because what we are going to hear from Opposition parties is the challenging of the Government’s position in this space.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Opposition parties will use their second-reading speeches to challenge the Government's position on offshore renewable energy.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the second reading debate on the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill (22 October 2025 onward): true if Opposition party speeches challenged the Government's position in this area, false if Opposition parties instead spoke in support of the bill and the Government's approach to it.

focus.statement: Let’s be very clear, because what we are going to hear from Opposition parties is the challenging of the Government’s position in this space.
focus.explanation: Embedded in an otherwise policy-heavy speech, but the content of this sentence is entirely an anticipation of what the other side will do rather than anything about the regime itself.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is something that we have spoken of not only in Government but, actually, in Opposition, when we stood on that policy of electrifying New Zealand, and that is the mandate we got in the last election—to bring bills like this through the House.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to electoral mandate: because the party campaigned on Electrify NZ and won, it concludes it has authority for this particular bill. The inference is a common but loose one — a general election result does not by itself establish endorsement of a specific measure — though the policy was genuinely campaigned on, so it is not empty.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: International developers are exploring offshore wind projects in New Zealand, and this bill will give them certainty to invest.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that offshore wind developers based overseas are currently investigating projects in New Zealand waters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE and company records of offshore wind feasibility activity in New Zealand as at October 2025 (e.g. announced feasibility studies or consortium filings by overseas developers in the South Taranaki Bight): true if one or more international developers had live offshore wind project investigations in New Zealand, false if no such developer activity existed.

veracity.statement: What we do know is that, under the last Government, the issue was around consents; there was interest, but obviously people were waiting—it was reported publicly—eight years for consents.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the 2017–2023 government, consenting for energy projects took as long as eight years, and that this was publicly reported.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published consenting timelines for New Zealand renewable energy projects between 2017 and 2023 (RMA consent lodgement to final determination, including Environment Court appeals, per MfE/MBIE or contemporaneous reporting): true if documented cases of consent processes lasting about eight years exist, false if the longest documented processes were materially shorter.

veracity.statement: It builds on work that was under way under the previous Government that was picked up and carried on with by the current Government, and it is much-needed legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that policy work on an offshore renewable energy regulatory regime began under the 2017–2023 government and was continued by the current government into this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE publications on offshore renewable energy before October 2023 (discussion documents, consultation papers, Cabinet papers) and the bill's own departmental disclosure statement: true if a regulatory regime for offshore renewable energy was under development before the change of government, false if the work began only after October 2023.

veracity.statement: Of course, we are experiencing, frankly, an over-abundance of wind today, and so I just want to recall in the House today that people in Canterbury, people in Kaikōura, people in Tasman-Nelson, and now people in Wellington are experiencing some pretty severe wind conditions today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the day of the speech severe wind was affecting Canterbury, Kaikōura, Tasman-Nelson and Wellington.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MetService severe weather warnings and recorded wind observations for 22 October 2025: true if strong or severe wind warnings were in force, or damaging gusts recorded, across those four areas that day; false if conditions were unremarkable.

specificity.statement: Permits will be “use it or lose it”, which I think is important with the provisions, meaning that, if a project fails to start or progress, the area can be made available to other developers.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete permitting mechanism and states its operative consequence — a lapsed area returning to availability — so the claim can be checked against the bill's text. No figures or timeframes, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister for Energy will consider commercial permit applications and must have regard to readiness to carry out the proposed development, compliance with requirements in the legislation, conditions of the applicant’s feasibility permit, and the applicant’s ability to put in place an acceptable financial security arrangement.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the decision-maker and enumerates the four statutory considerations that bind the decision; directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What we do know is that, under the last Government, the issue was around consents; there was interest, but obviously people were waiting—it was reported publicly—eight years for consents.
civility.explanation: Criticises the previous government's consenting record squarely as a record; no individual's character, competence or motives are impugned.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s about 40 percent of the time in, say, the Ruahine wind farms and things like that, and the offshore wind farms can turn pretty much all of the time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two capacity-factor claims: that New Zealand onshore wind farms such as those in the Ruahine range generate roughly 40 percent of the time, and that offshore wind turbines generate essentially continuously.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Transpower generation statistics for NZ onshore wind capacity factor (true if the onshore figure is near 40%, false if materially different), and published offshore wind capacity factors from IEA/IRENA (the offshore claim is true only if offshore capacity factors approach 100%, false if they sit in the typical 40-60% band).

veracity.statement: Those two uses are going to be particularly difficult to put together, but here we have reports from October 2024—so about this time a year ago—of wind power firm BlueFloat Energy cancelling its plan for wind farms in New Zealand, and the major reason was that a seabed mining firm wanted to mine offshore from the south coast of Taranaki.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that BlueFloat Energy cancelled its New Zealand offshore wind plans in October 2024, and that the principal reason was a competing seabed mining proposal off the south Taranaki coast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: BlueFloat Energy's own statements and NZ media reporting from October 2024; true if BlueFloat withdrew from its NZ projects at that time AND cited the competing South Taranaki Bight seabed mining project as the main reason, false if the withdrawal happened at a different time or was attributed principally to other causes (e.g. group-level financing or its parent's global retrenchment).

veracity.statement: However, we do have some things to say about this bill given that the Government is promoting fast track as a solution to everything, and we’ve seen what happens with fast track with Trans-Tasman Resources being written into the legislation and BlueFloat floating away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Trans-Tasman Resources' seabed mining project was written into the fast-track legislation itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 as enacted; true if the Trans-Tasman Resources / Taranaki VTM project is named in the schedule of listed projects, false if it is absent from the Act and was only referred in by later Ministerial decision.

veracity.statement: You can’t build wind turbines without minerals.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wind turbine construction necessarily requires mined mineral inputs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published material composition data for utility-scale wind turbines (e.g. IEA/USGS bills of materials); true if steel, copper and rare-earth or other mined inputs are required in every current turbine design, false if a commercially deployed mineral-free turbine exists.

veracity.statement: We see in Scandinavia wooden wind turbine towers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wind turbine towers made of wood are in use in Scandinavia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records of laminated-timber wind turbine towers installed in Sweden, Norway or Denmark (e.g. Modvion's installations); true if at least one wooden tower is erected and operating there, false if the technology exists only as a prototype or proposal.

specificity.statement: Those two uses are going to be particularly difficult to put together, but here we have reports from October 2024—so about this time a year ago—of wind power firm BlueFloat Energy cancelling its plan for wind farms in New Zealand, and the major reason was that a seabed mining firm wanted to mine offshore from the south coast of Taranaki.
specificity.explanation: Names the firm, the month and year, the action taken and the stated cause, and locates it geographically. Someone could go and check every element of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They are jobs where our sparkies can be employed, where our engineers can be employed, and where workers of all sorts can have work to do that actually really contributes to the country, that is well-paid, and that gives that sense of standing—the sense that when they get up and go to work in the morning, they are doing a job that is worth doing.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance about the employment case for offshore wind, but carries no numbers, no timeframe and no mechanism — only broad trade categories and generic virtues (well-paid, worthwhile, a sense of standing).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is time that we focused on the renewables transition we want rather than simply seeking to extract more minerals and destroy our reputation internationally.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no content attached: no mechanism, no figure, no named measure, and no statement of what focusing on the transition would actually involve.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is part of the work that we must do to become an energy-independent nation, and that’s a great goal for us to have. Why? Because we do not want to be dependent on overseas fuel suppliers.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the reason offered for pursuing energy independence is that we do not want to depend on overseas suppliers, which restates the goal rather than supporting it. No cost, security or supply-risk premise is offered to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, we do have some things to say about this bill given that the Government is promoting fast track as a solution to everything, and we’ve seen what happens with fast track with Trans-Tasman Resources being written into the legislation and BlueFloat floating away.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal leap: the listing of a seabed mining project and BlueFloat's departure are placed side by side and treated as cause and effect, with nothing offered to link them beyond sequence. There is a genuine policy inference here, but a weak one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is time that we focused on the renewables transition we want rather than simply seeking to extract more minerals and destroy our reputation internationally.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: renewables and mineral extraction are presented as mutually exclusive paths, when renewable build-out is itself mineral-intensive — the point Simon Court makes immediately afterwards. The inference concerns the policy, but the disjunction is not established.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However, we do have some things to say about this bill given that the Government is promoting fast track as a solution to everything, and we’ve seen what happens with fast track with Trans-Tasman Resources being written into the legislation and BlueFloat floating away.
focus.explanation: Names a specific statute, a specific listed project and a specific consequence — that is scrutiny, not tribalism — but it is framed by the sweeping party characterisation that the Government promotes fast track "as a solution to everything", which carries some of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are used to the trivial nature of the Government.
focus.explanation: A blanket characterisation of the Government's general seriousness. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — pure party framing, which is exactly what Focus exists to catch. It insults no individual, so Civility is untouched.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I would have loved to have done was spend some time in the Cabinet when this bill was being discussed, because I wonder how the Hon Shane Jones was able to manage the restrictions we require on extraction to enable the offshore renewables transition.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and insinuates something about how he handled the extraction restrictions, without stating it or attacking his character or competence directly. Pointed and robust, edging toward the person but not landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are still risks if there are multiple uses in that area, and these risks don’t magically disappear when we limit some things, because if we’ve got large boats that are seeking to operate in the area, we have risks to big bits of kit—to our wind turbines.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference about the measure: co-location of shipping and turbines in the same area creates collision risk, so partial use limits do not remove residual risk. The mechanism is named and the conclusion tracks it, but no evidence or magnitude is offered for how much risk survives the controls, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is really problematic because we've been told that this Government wants to double or triple renewable electricity generation, yet it can't deliver on time the legislation we need to meet that target.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference on its own terms: if the stated target requires the enabling instruments, and those instruments are overdue, the target is at risk. The gap is that no link is established between the missing NPS/NES and the actual rate of generation build — the earlier point that the 2011 NPS made no difference arguably cuts against the premise that the instrument is what the target depends on.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a focus to make sure not only that we build the renewables we need but that we involve the communities that are affected in those buildings.
specificity.explanation: A statement of intent with no mechanism, threshold, timeframe or figure: no indication of how communities would be involved, at what stage, or with what effect. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is really, really important because at the moment, the $10 billion per annum of fossil fuels we import costs us, costs everybody, costs every household heavily, in a cost of living crisis.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete, checkable figure — a dollar amount and a period ($10 billion per annum, on fossil fuel imports). Falls short of the top because the claimed consequence for households is asserted without any per-household amount or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We had a promise that we would have national environmental standards. That still has not been delivered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things: that the current Government committed to producing national environmental standards for renewable electricity generation, and that as at 22 October 2025 no such standards had been made.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment announcements and work programme timetables for the National Environmental Standards for renewable electricity generation, plus the New Zealand Gazette record. True if a commitment to deliver NES-REG is documented and no NES had been gazetted by 22 October 2025; false if the standards had been gazetted by that date, or if no such commitment was made.

veracity.statement: There was the Board of Inquiry into the Proposed National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation in 2010. It was gazetted and implemented in 2011.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a Board of Inquiry considered the proposed National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation in 2010, and that the NPS was gazetted and took effect in 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Board of Inquiry report on the Proposed NPS for Renewable Electricity Generation and the New Zealand Gazette notice for the NPS-REG. True if the Board of Inquiry reported in 2010 and the NPS was gazetted in 2011; false if either date is materially different.

veracity.statement: Since then, numerous reviews of the national policy statement for renewable electricity generation have made it really clear that it made no impact whatsoever in enabling renewable electricity generation through the Resource Management Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that multiple published reviews of the NPS-REG concluded it had no effect at all on enabling renewable electricity generation under the RMA. The absolute form — 'no impact whatsoever' — is part of what is being claimed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluations of the NPS-REG (Ministry for the Environment / MBIE effectiveness reviews, Environment Court and consent-decision analyses). True if multiple reviews conclude the NPS-REG had no discernible effect on consenting outcomes; false if reviews find some enabling effect, or if only a single review exists, or if the reviews' finding is 'limited/insufficient' rather than 'none'.

veracity.statement: This is really, really important because at the moment, the $10 billion per annum of fossil fuels we import costs us, costs everybody, costs every household heavily, in a cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's annual imports of fossil fuels are worth approximately $10 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade statistics for imports of petroleum and petroleum products (plus coal), annual value for the year to 2025. True if the total is approximately $10 billion NZD; false if materially different (e.g. below $7b or above $13b).

divination.statement: I think we will need to improve it when we take Government in 2026, but at least this gives us something to work on.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the speaker's party will be part of the government formed after the 2026 New Zealand general election. This is an electoral outcome determined by voters, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The composition of the government formed after the 2026 New Zealand general election, per the Governor-General's appointment of Ministers and any coalition or confidence-and-supply agreements. True if the Green Party is in government (in Cabinet or as a support party with ministerial portfolios); false if it sits on the opposition benches.

specificity.statement: This bill fixes what matters. It provides certainty over ambiguity, pace over drift, and, above all, accountability over open-ended process.
specificity.explanation: A string of abstract contrasts — certainty, pace, accountability — with no figure, mechanism, clause or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The next action, consistent with my delegation from the Minister for Resource Management Reform, is to deliver an environmental management framework for offshore wind that provides a clear and reasonable consenting pathway across the coastal and marine area.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete deliverable and its scope (an environmental management framework covering the coastal and marine area, under a named delegation), but supplies no date, no standards and no thresholds — the direction is clear, the how much and by when are not.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, proponents of renewable projects have told me, and I know they will have told other members of this House and the Government, that without reliable thermal firming, the type of renewable energy projects like offshore wind simply won’t get off the ground, because those developers cannot sell offshore wind or any other type of renewable to their customers unless they have an insurance policy in thermal firming to back it up.
rigor.explanation: A genuine causal argument (intermittent generation is unsellable without firming, so firming is a precondition for investment), but the whole support is an appeal to unnamed authority — 'proponents have told me' — with no contract, market or modelling evidence offered. Real inference, real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While he proposes you can build wind turbines with sticks and bits of wood, I tell you what: the wind turbines coming out of North America, Europe, and China right now are made out of critical minerals; they’re made out of epoxy resins made from oil and gas and coal.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. No Green member proposed wooden turbines; the position attacked was not the position held, so refuting it establishes nothing about the seabed-minerals argument actually in dispute. Scored here, not under Civility — the target is the argument, not the man.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealand must be at least as bankable as our neighbours in Australia because developers will judge whether to invest in Australia, if it’s easier, or New Zealand, if it’s easier.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise — if capital is mobile between two jurisdictions, the harder regime loses projects — but the premise is asserted rather than shown, and 'bankable' is doing unexamined work. A sound shape with an unevidenced middle.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, proponents of renewable projects have told me, and I know they will have told other members of this House and the Government, that without reliable thermal firming, the type of renewable energy projects like offshore wind simply won’t get off the ground, because those developers cannot sell offshore wind or any other type of renewable to their customers unless they have an insurance policy in thermal firming to back it up.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the energy system the bill sits in — firming, developer offtake, project viability. High focus alongside mediocre rigor: arguing thinly about the actual policy is still on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The wishful thinking of the Labour Party, since announcing a just transition and cancelling an entire industry like offshore oil and gas exploration, is like giving people a pink slip and a pat on the head and a “wish you well”.
focus.explanation: A real policy target is named — the just transition and the offshore exploration decision — but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the other party's attitude rather than an engagement with what the policy did or cost.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s why ACT is trusted with important work streams in this Government.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome — the content is the standing of his own party within the coalition. Party framing rather than the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: While he proposes you can build wind turbines with sticks and bits of wood, I tell you what: the wind turbines coming out of North America, Europe, and China right now are made out of critical minerals; they’re made out of epoxy resins made from oil and gas and coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that utility-scale wind turbines currently manufactured in North America, Europe and China depend on critical minerals and on epoxy resins derived from oil, gas and coal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Manufacturer and IEA/USGS material-composition data for utility-scale wind turbines produced in North America, Europe and China: true if such turbines routinely incorporate critical minerals (rare-earth permanent magnets, copper, alloying elements) and petrochemical-derived epoxy composite blades; false if commercially produced turbines from those regions are typically built without either.

veracity.statement: Now, we should also learn from Australia, particularly our cousins in Victoria, where declared areas for offshore renewables and transparent milestones give developers clarity and give communities confidence about what’s coming next.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Victorian/Australian offshore renewables regime operates through formally declared areas and published milestones.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Declaration instruments made under Australia's Offshore Electricity Infrastructure Act 2021 covering waters off Victoria (e.g. the Gippsland declared area) and the Victorian Government's offshore wind implementation statements: true if declared areas exist there with published milestone or auction timetables; false if no area has been declared or no milestone timetable published.

veracity.statement: The wishful thinking of the Labour Party, since announcing a just transition and cancelling an entire industry like offshore oil and gas exploration, is like giving people a pink slip and a pat on the head and a “wish you well”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour's offshore oil and gas decision cancelled an entire industry, and that displaced workers were given nothing beyond good wishes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown Minerals (Petroleum) Amendment Act 2018 and MBIE permit/production data: true if offshore petroleum exploration and production ceased as a result; false if existing exploration and mining permits remained in force and offshore production continued after 2018. Transition support is checkable against the Just Transitions Taranaki programme's funded outputs.

veracity.statement: You promised it in June last year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government committed in June 2024 to delivering the national policy statements for renewable electricity generation and electricity networks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial announcements and the resource management national direction work programme as published in June 2024: true if a commitment to deliver a national policy statement for renewable electricity generation was made that month; false if no such June 2024 commitment is on record.

civility.statement: Look, just to reflect back on something we often hear from the Greens, educate yourself greenies, because you can’t have one without the other.
civility.explanation: 'Educate yourself greenies' is condescension aimed at the members opposite rather than at their case — it asserts ignorance instead of answering it. Short of a direct insult, but past the point of civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I understand that the Minister for Resource Management Reform, Chris Bishop, will have more to say about the results of that consultation in the near future, and I’m sure it will address many of the concerns that the Green Party member had, no matter how misinformed.
civility.explanation: 'No matter how misinformed' dismisses a named member's concerns by attributing ignorance to him rather than engaging what he said. Condescension toward the person, not criticism of the position.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The fast-track bill: I do want to speak about that, as we hear often in the House about the fast-track bill and, at the moment, I think there’s 22 renewable projects in the fast-track bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 22 of the projects listed under the fast-track approvals regime are renewable energy projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The schedule of listed projects in the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (and any subsequent referrals), counting those classified as renewable electricity generation (wind, solar, hydro); true if the count is 22 at the date of the statement, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The first term of the Labour Government was a New Zealand First coalition Government, with supply and confidence from the Green Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the constitutional form of the 2017–2020 government: a Labour–New Zealand First coalition, with the Green Party outside Cabinet on a confidence and supply arrangement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2017 Labour–New Zealand First coalition agreement and the Labour–Green confidence and supply agreement as lodged/published after the 2017 election; true if NZ First was the coalition partner and the Greens provided confidence and supply, false if either party's status differed.

veracity.statement: Australia has set a very aggressive and impressive emissions reduction target of 62 percent to 70 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Australia's emissions reduction target is a 62–70 percent reduction (implicitly its 2035 nationally determined contribution).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australia's 2035 nationally determined contribution as submitted to the UNFCCC; true if the headline range is 62–70% below the stated baseline year, false if the range is materially different.

veracity.statement: One of the things that they took away when they first came into office was the decarbonising industry fund, which was a really important component.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on taking office the current Government discontinued a fund for decarbonising industry (the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry / GIDI fund).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and EECA/MBIE announcements on the status of the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry fund; true if new funding was discontinued by the incoming Government, false if it was retained.

focus.statement: It is disappointing, as we’ve gone through fast track, that the Opposition parties have not realised the potential to actually get some runs on the board, especially in the renewable space.
focus.explanation: A real policy referent (the fast-track regime and renewable projects) but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the Opposition parties' general posture rather than a named measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you look at the things like the Regulatory Standards Bill, if you look at the Treaty principles bill, if you look at charter schools—if you look at all sorts of legislation—we definitely agree with them that ACT has definitely been a powerful and driving influence on this Government.
focus.explanation: Named measures are cited, which lifts it off the floor, but the point being made is about another party's influence within the Government rather than about any policy's mechanism, cost or effect — and it is a digression from the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, that’s why we’ve called on them to not reverse the oil and gas ban, because one of the things we need to do is give confidence to people who want to invest in New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy (the offshore oil and gas exploration ban) and the position taken on it, with a stated policy rationale.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the things that they took away when they first came into office was the decarbonising industry fund, which was a really important component.
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme and a specific decision taken on it. Scrutiny of a named government action, not party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is disappointing, as we’ve gone through fast track, that the Opposition parties have not realised the potential to actually get some runs on the board, especially in the renewable space.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested criticism of opponents that lands on their collective position, not on any individual; no imputation of bad faith or personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That isn’t going to give confidence to renewable energy, just as it has in other sectors when people say things like that: “Oh, maybe further down the track, we’ll really look at this and decline things”—that won’t give confidence to investors to come here and invest.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the policy: signalling that consents may later be revisited deters investment. The support is an unspecified analogy to 'other sectors' — a plausible but unevidenced appeal to a parallel case, leaving a gap between what is offered and the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, that’s why we’ve called on them to not reverse the oil and gas ban, because one of the things we need to do is give confidence to people who want to invest in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — policy stability produces investor confidence, therefore do not reverse the ban — but it elides the step that reversing a ban could equally raise confidence among a different class of investor. A real gap between premise and conclusion rather than a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Through this bill, we see that it’s just a two-stage permitting regime.
specificity.explanation: Names an actual mechanism in the bill (a two-stage permitting regime) and is checkable against the text, but carries no figures, thresholds or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think you could look at it something like spatial planning; in the Resource Management Act, we look at spatial planning on the land, and maybe here we need spatial planning in the sea, so it’s that same kind of concept.
specificity.explanation: Borrows a named concept from named legislation, which gives it some purchase, but proposes no instrument, no allocation rule and no timeframe — 'maybe here we need spatial planning in the sea' commits to nothing operational.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Australia has set a very aggressive and impressive emissions reduction target of 62 percent to 70 percent.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise, checkable numeric range for a named country's target; short of full marks only because the baseline year and target year are left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In that regard, we do want to give policy certainty, and the policy certainty we do want to give, which is partly being granted through this bill, is for investors to come to New Zealand, invest in offshore renewable energy, and invest in renewable energy in general, and not to invest in the declining sunset fossil gas industry, because that’s not something that’s going to be continued and supported across the next Government.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the government formed after the next general election will not continue policy support for the oil and gas industry.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The coalition/confidence agreements and first-year energy policy decisions of the government formed after the 2026 New Zealand general election; true if that government withdraws or does not maintain support for oil and gas exploration (e.g. does not fund or promote new exploration and does not retain the 2024 reinstatement of permitting), false if it continues or extends that support.

veracity.statement: I’m glad to report—Madam Speaker, you may be interested in this—that Reefton is now back on, and all substations are also back on across the top of the South and the West Coast.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, as at the morning of 22 October 2025, power had been restored to Reefton and that all substations across the top of the South Island and the West Coast were back on.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Outage records/restoration notices from the relevant lines companies (Network Tasman, Marlborough Lines, Buller Electricity/Westpower) and Transpower for 22 October 2025; true if Reefton supply and all named-region substations were restored by that morning, false if any remained off.

veracity.statement: New Zealand implemented similar mechanisms for oil and gas in 2021 through amendments to the Crown Minerals Act 1991.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that decommissioning obligations backed by financial security arrangements were introduced for oil and gas by 2021 amendments to the Crown Minerals Act 1991.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enactment record for the Crown Minerals (Decommissioning and Other Matters) Amendment Act 2021 on legislation.govt.nz; true if it was enacted in 2021 and imposes decommissioning and financial-security obligations on permit/licence holders, false if no such 2021 amendment exists or it lacks those mechanisms.

veracity.statement: The committee received 71 written submissions and 21 oral submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts precise submission counts for the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's consideration of the offshore renewable energy bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The committee's report on the bill (and the submissions list on parliament.nz); true if 71 written and 21 oral submissions are recorded, false if the recorded numbers differ materially.

rigor.statement: This exclusivity is vital. It provides a secure window for developers to undertake the complexity and costly feasibility studies and apply for the necessary environmental consents.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about the measure: exclusive feasibility permits are justified because feasibility studies are costly and need a protected window. The step follows, but 'vital' is stronger than what is offered — no reason is given why exclusivity is necessary rather than merely helpful, so there is a gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill enables safety zones of up to 500 metres to be established around offshore renewable generation infrastructure and substations, and this will prohibit unauthorised people or vessels from entering or undertaking certain activity in that area.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — a named mechanism in the bill and what it does. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill also includes a range of offenses and penalties for breaches of the regime, from $3,000 to $10 million in fines, through permit revocation or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.
specificity.explanation: Concrete and checkable: fine range, the alternative sanctions, and a maximum custodial term. Someone could verify it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill does more than set up a regime for offshore renewable energy; it creates an economy that is going to be powered by clean energy.
specificity.explanation: A peroration claim with no figure, mechanism, share or timeframe attached — 'an economy powered by clean energy' commits to nothing checkable, in contrast to the detailed permit and penalty provisions described earlier.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The billions of dollars in private investment that this framework attracts will translate directly to demand for engineers, specialised marine technicians, and other high-value jobs.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the regulatory framework will attract private investment in the billions of dollars into New Zealand offshore renewable energy, and that this will generate specialised engineering and marine technical employment.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Committed private capital in New Zealand offshore renewable energy projects under the feasibility/commercial permit regime, per MBIE permit records and developers' announced final investment decisions; true if cumulative committed private investment reaches NZ$1 billion or more with associated construction/operations hiring, false if it remains below that or no project reaches a final investment decision.

civility.statement: I mean, I’m not targeting anyone in this, because I think successive Governments have dropped the ball or haven’t actually been ahead of the ball.
civility.explanation: Allocates blame for a genuinely contested failure — a real opportunity to be uncivil — and explicitly declines to aim it at any person, including his own side in the criticism.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, this is a good bill, but you wouldn’t get that, necessarily, from listening to the speech of the previous member, Glen Bennett. He brought up so many “if”, “but”, and “what” questions, which made you question whether this is a good bill.
civility.explanation: Pointed and directed at a named member, but the target is the content and tone of his speech rather than his character or competence; it edges toward the person without landing on them. No Rigor score: strip out the characterisation of the other member and no argument remains.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can tell the member Mr Court, perhaps as he casts his eyes towards Australia, he can wave the Taranaki workforce goodbye, because, in that time, that’s what’s happened.
civility.explanation: Robust and personally directed at a named member, implying inattention or misplaced focus, but stops short of impugning his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was just under $450 million of taxpayers’ money that was spent in terms of the decommissioning.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the total Crown expenditure on decommissioning the Tūī oil field was slightly under NZ$450 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown/MBIE and Treasury appropriations and reporting on the Tūī field decommissioning programme; true if the total Crown spend is between roughly $400m and $450m, false if materially outside that range (e.g. under $300m or over $500m).

veracity.statement: Of course, we’ve had BlueFloat who were there, who were in the mix and have pulled out, have moved on, because of the challenges of getting the regime and getting the settings right.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that BlueFloat Energy was pursuing an offshore wind development in New Zealand, has since withdrawn, and that regulatory uncertainty was the reason.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: BlueFloat Energy company announcements and NZ media/MBIE records on its New Zealand offshore wind interest; true if BlueFloat had an active NZ offshore wind project and publicly exited before 22 October 2025, with regulatory/permitting uncertainty cited as a reason; false if it never held such a project, is still active, or gave unrelated reasons (e.g. global divestment) for leaving.

veracity.statement: It was already in train when we were in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that work on an offshore renewable energy regulatory regime had already begun under the previous Labour Government, before the current Government took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's offshore renewable energy work programme records — discussion documents, consultation rounds and Cabinet papers dated before October 2023; true if substantive regulatory development on offshore renewable energy was under way before the change of Government, false if the work began only after it.

rigor.statement: We don’t want that to happen again, because we know that the purse strings in the Treasury are tight. We know that we need to be investing money in clean energy, into things like health, into homes, into making sure that we have good jobs.
rigor.explanation: A genuine opportunity-cost inference: fiscal constraint plus competing calls on the same money supports the conclusion that the Crown should not absorb another operator's decommissioning bill. No fallacy; the small gap is that the premise about competing spending is asserted rather than quantified.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The other one, just finally, is around the purchasing of permits and what that looks like. We need to reflect on that, because we don’t want this legislation to enable someone to be able to buy a patch of ocean floor, hold on to it—you know, invest not in infrastructure, not in building any wind turbines, but sitting on it—to be able to sell in the future and to make a profit, and nothing to actually be done.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific mechanism in the bill before the House — the permit-purchase regime and the risk of speculative permit-holding — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My advice to any overseas investor that wants to come here is that you beat a path to all stakeholders in Taranaki and make sure that those relationships are strong and that they are active in allowing that investment to move forward; failure to do so would be a mistake, and, actually, it should not be a tick-box exercise through this legislation.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at how the legislation should handle iwi and stakeholder engagement — a substantive feature of the regime — rather than at any party's record.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a bill that’s about saying yes: yes to jobs, yes to economic growth, yes to foreign investment, yes to energy security, and yes to meeting our climate commitments.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So we did make a number of changes to the bill around the feasibility permits, changing the permitting regime, making sure that the decommissioning obligations were clarified, including being clear about what infrastructure is excluded as part of the feasibility and commission regime, and also dealing with the competing offshore renewable energy applications and how that was to be addressed.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete areas of amendment (feasibility permits, permitting regime, decommissioning obligations, competing applications), but gives no clause numbers, figures or detail of what the changes actually say.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s also good news for the guardians of the New Zealand Super Fund, which, of course, have in their guardianship over $85 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the New Zealand Superannuation Fund held more than NZ$85 billion in assets under management as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Super Fund monthly performance report / annual report for the period around October 2025; true if reported net fund value exceeds NZ$85 billion, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: New Zealand has not currently got a regulatory regime for offshore renewable energy, and so we are progressing this legislation to fix that and to enable this new form of energy generation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, as at October 2025, New Zealand had no dedicated regulatory regime governing offshore renewable energy developments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE offshore renewable energy policy documents and the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill's explanatory note / regulatory impact statement; true if they state no dedicated permitting regime existed prior to the Bill, false if an existing offshore renewable permitting regime is identified.

veracity.statement: I’m really pleased that the House had the opportunity to hear from my colleague the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe to correct the record, really, that this is a piece of work that Labour started because of our commitment to unlocking the potential for renewables, and it has been picked up by this Government, which we are really happy about.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the policy work underlying the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill was begun under the previous Labour government and continued by the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE offshore renewable energy consultation documents and Cabinet papers dated before October 2023; true if the regulatory work programme was initiated under the Labour government, false if the work began only after the change of government.

veracity.statement: So what that means is that it’s equal to some of our largest hydro stations and more than eight Harapaki Wind Farms combined.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that up to 1 GW of offshore wind is equivalent to some of New Zealand's largest hydro stations and to more than eight Harapaki Wind Farms combined.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Installed capacity of Harapaki Wind Farm (Meridian) and of the largest NZ hydro stations (Manapōuri, Benmore) from the generators' published figures; true if 1 GW exceeds eight times Harapaki's capacity (or eight times its annual generation, if that basis is used), false if 1 GW is materially fewer than eight Harapaki equivalents.

veracity.statement: I just thought I’d mention it’s rather ironic, with all the wind we have outside at the moment, that a lot of the turbines would not actually be able to operate because they turn off at 90 kilometres an hour or thereabouts, and I think there’s been some wind speeds in excess of 200 kilometres now in the South Island today.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that wind turbines cut out at around 90 km/h, and that South Island wind speeds exceeded 200 km/h on 22 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Turbine manufacturer specifications for cut-out wind speed (typically stated in m/s) and MetService/NIWA recorded maximum gusts for South Island stations on 22 October 2025; true if cut-out is ~25 m/s (~90 km/h) and a recorded gust exceeded 200 km/h that day, false if either figure is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Now, if we think about the current stored generating capacity of all the wind turbines in New Zealand at the moment just being north of one gigawatt, this one farm can be actually immense—huge, in fact.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that total installed wind generation capacity in New Zealand is a little over one gigawatt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Energy in New Zealand / Electricity Authority installed generation capacity figures for wind as at 2025; true if total installed wind capacity is between roughly 1.0 and 1.4 GW, false if materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: It’s recently been established that you can easily have gigawatts of wind generation and the potential of the Trans-Tasman Resources proposal existing together.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that recent analysis has shown multi-gigawatt offshore wind generation and the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining proposal can coexist in the South Taranaki Bight.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A published spatial or technical assessment (MBIE, the offshore wind developers, TTR, or the fast-track consenting documents) covering overlap between the TTR permit area and viable offshore wind areas; true if such an assessment concludes coexistence is feasible, false if no such assessment exists or it finds material conflict.

specificity.statement: So, look, the National Party are committed to this as part of our Electrify New Zealand, which of course is all about the goal of doubling renewable energy generation by 2050—we are now delivering.
specificity.explanation: Names a policy programme (Electrify New Zealand) and a quantified target with a date (doubling renewable generation by 2050), but supplies no mechanism, cost or interim milestone; "we are now delivering" carries no checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I won’t repeat all the comments made by previous members—I think we’ve got the message loud and clear that this is a pretty good bill—apart from to put into context the importance of the Taranaki wind farm developments, because what it will do with that offshore wind project is generate up to 1 gigawatt of electricity, and that’s equal to 1 billion watts.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete generation figure for a named project and converts the unit so it can be checked and compared; stops short of a timeframe or cost.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is around clarifying how maritime space conflicts will be managed in terms of mining and aquaculture; it’s about strengthening environmental compliance obligations under exclusive economic zone and Resource Management Act frameworks; and as my colleague the Rt Hon Adrian has said, enhancing Treaty of Waitangi recognition and Māori engagement.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete areas of the regime to be tested, identifies the competing uses (mining, aquaculture) and the statutory frameworks (EEZ, RMA); no figures or amendment wording, but each item is checkable against the Bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They need to install the pile-driven turbines in drafts less than 60 metres deep, and the South Taranaki Bight happens to have an immense amount of area.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete engineering constraint (pile-driven foundations below 60 metres depth) but quantifies the available seabed only as "an immense amount of area".
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course, despite what the Opposition may tell you on the black and white tiles, we are committed—National’s committed, this Government is committed—to meeting New Zealand’s long-term energy needs, hence why you’re hearing a lot about the energy sector coming from this Government.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy area (long-term energy needs) but the weight of the sentence is a pre-emptive swipe at what "the Opposition may tell you" plus a general assertion of commitment; no measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We will be keeping a close eye on that, given that sometimes we see one side of the ledger enhanced and enabled under Christopher Luxon’s Government without the surrounding protections and safeguards to ensure that the transitions can happen.
focus.explanation: A real policy concern (whether enabling provisions come with matching safeguards) but delivered as an unnamed general pattern attributed to the Government rather than tied to a specific measure or instance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s critically important that, at the earliest possible moment, proposals such as these start with conversations with iwi.
focus.explanation: Squarely about how the regime should operate — the sequencing of iwi engagement in the permitting process — with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, if we think about the current stored generating capacity of all the wind turbines in New Zealand at the moment just being north of one gigawatt, this one farm can be actually immense—huge, in fact.
rigor.explanation: A straightforward quantitative comparison — a single proposed farm of up to 2 GW against a national fleet of just over 1 GW — and the conclusion that the project is very large follows directly from the two figures offered. No fallacy; the only gap is that capacity and output are used loosely.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Government in the last two years has seen FENZ introduce an asset management plan, which had not been put in place, for some reason, between 2017 and 2023 after FENZ was formed from the voluntary and professional wings of New Zealand’s firefighting.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that FENZ had no asset management plan between its 2017 formation and 2023, and that one was introduced under the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ annual reports, Statements of Performance Expectations and Auditor-General/Ministerial reviews 2017-2025; true if no asset management plan existed before 2023 and one was adopted 2023-2025, false if a plan is documented in the 2017-2023 period.

veracity.statement: In total, FENZ is spending around $20 million to $25 million each year on upgrading fire appliances.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual FENZ capital spend on fire appliance upgrades of $20-25 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ annual report capital expenditure disclosures for fleet/appliances for the most recent financial years; true if annual appliance spend falls in the $20-25m range, false if materially outside it.

veracity.statement: It’s the first time that there has been a reduction of harm to children in State care, as we understand it, in the country’s history.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the recorded fall in harm to children in Oranga Tamariki residences is unprecedented in New Zealand's history.
veracity.subject: speaker
