civility.explanation: A condescending rebuke that imputes self-righteousness and hypocrisy to other members, edging past the argument and onto the people making it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And in relation to the second part, it’s always worth the House’s time repealing dumb legislation.
civility.explanation: Dismissive, but the target is the legislation, not any member. Hard criticism of a policy is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we want on this debate is sincerity, understanding, and insight, and not virtue signalling.
focus.explanation: Characterises the motives of the other side of the House. No policy, measure or outcome is named; remove the swipe at opponents and nothing about the motion remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Stop lecturing to us as though, somehow, they’re perfect and the rest of us are not.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side are 'really like'. Nothing in it engages the motion on Gaza and Israel that is before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And in relation to the second part, it’s always worth the House’s time repealing dumb legislation.
focus.explanation: Gestures at legislation, but names no bill, provision or outcome; the weight of it is a swipe at the previous government's statute book rather than a policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, we would like to see a ceasefire, but in order to achieve a sustainable ceasefire, as the member well knows, both sides actually need to be able to do so, and that means that they both have to agree to be able to put down their arms, they both have to actually agree to cease fighting across the whole area of the conflict in Gaza and in Israel, both parties actually need to commit to a political process and a peace process to resolve their differences, and both sides need to take those steps in order to get those conditions in place.
focus.explanation: Answers the policy question put to him about the Government's ceasefire position, setting out the conditions it turns on. No party framing and no reference to the questioner's record.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, we would like to see a ceasefire, but in order to achieve a sustainable ceasefire, as the member well knows, both sides actually need to be able to do so, and that means that they both have to agree to be able to put down their arms, they both have to actually agree to cease fighting across the whole area of the conflict in Gaza and in Israel, both parties actually need to commit to a political process and a peace process to resolve their differences, and both sides need to take those steps in order to get those conditions in place.
rigor.explanation: The premises describe what it would take to achieve a durable ceasefire; the conclusion drawn is that New Zealand should not join an immediate call for one. That is a non sequitur — it conflates bringing a ceasefire about with advocating for it, and the stated conditions do not bear on whether a call should be made.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Why won’t the New Zealand Government call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire when more than 16,000 people have died, the great majority of them civilians, and that is continuing as we speak?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a cumulative death toll of more than 16,000 in Gaza as at 7 December 2023, and that civilians are the great majority of those deaths.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gaza Ministry of Health / UN OCHA cumulative fatality figures reported for 6-7 December 2023; true if the reported toll exceeds 16,000 and the reported women-and-children share is a clear majority, false if the toll was materially below 16,000 at that date.

veracity.statement: The official cash rate is at its highest level in 15 years, pushing mortgage interest rates over 7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the OCR in December 2023 was at a 15-year high, and that retail mortgage interest rates had passed 7 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ official cash rate series — true if the December 2023 OCR level had not been equalled or exceeded at any point since December 2008, false if it had; plus RBNZ retail mortgage rate series, true if advertised/effective fixed rates exceeded 7 percent.

veracity.statement: The Government books are in deficit and are burdened by more debt than at any point since 1995.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Crown debt in late 2023 was at its highest level since 1995 — on the debt-to-GDP framing she uses later in the same answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's long-run fiscal time series for net core Crown debt as a share of GDP; true if the 2023 ratio exceeds every annual observation from 1995 onward, false if any year since 1995 records a higher ratio. The claim's truth depends on which debt measure is used, so check both net core Crown debt and the post-2022 net debt measure.

veracity.statement: The Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update showed that New Zealand is expected to run a deficit of $11.4 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific forecast deficit figure for the 2023/24 year to a named Treasury document.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2023, forecast OBEGAL for the 2023/24 year; true if that figure is a deficit of approximately $11.4 billion, false if materially different or if the figure comes from a different measure or year.

veracity.statement: Previous promises made by the outgoing Minister of Finance to reduce Government spending after the pandemic—those promises were broken, with Government spending this financial year substantially higher than at any time during the pandemic, including periods where large parts of the country were locked down and businesses forcibly closed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that core Crown expenditure in 2023/24 is substantially higher than in any pandemic year, and that this contradicts commitments given by the previous Minister of Finance to wind spending back.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series for 2019/20 through 2023/24; true if the 2023/24 figure exceeds every pandemic-year figure by a clear margin, false if any pandemic year matches or exceeds it. Separately, Budget speeches and fiscal strategy statements 2020-2023 for the stated commitment to reduce spending post-pandemic.

veracity.statement: Dairy farmers across the country will be pleased with the news today that Fonterra have increased their forecast farm-gate milk price by 25c to $7.50—better times ahead.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Fonterra announced, on or about 7 December 2023, a 25 cent lift in its forecast farm-gate milk price to $7.50.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fonterra's forecast farmgate milk price announcements for the 2023/24 season; true if a revision announced in the first week of December 2023 raised the midpoint by 25c to $7.50/kgMS, false if the size, level or date differ.

veracity.statement: Well, yes, I have, and our Government might have inherited challenging economic conditions, but, clearly, our election has given many reason for hope, because ANZ’s Business Outlook shows business confidence is already higher than at any point during the last Government’s tenure. In fact, it’s at its highest level since March 2015.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the ANZ Business Outlook confidence reading is higher than at any point from late 2017 to late 2023, and is the highest since March 2015.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: ANZ Business Outlook headline business confidence series; true if the November 2023 reading exceeds every monthly reading from October 2017 onward and is not exceeded by any reading after March 2015, false if any intervening month is higher.

veracity.statement: What I can tell the House is that debt has gone in New Zealand—Government debt has gone from $5.4 billion up to $100 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rise in government debt from $5.4 billion to $100 billion, without naming the debt measure or the start and end dates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury net core Crown debt and the post-2022 net debt measure, 2017 and 2023 (and the PREFU 2023 forecast track); true if some consistent published measure runs from about $5.4 billion to about $100 billion across the stated period, false if no single measure supports both endpoints.

veracity.statement: Is he committed to the principles in his coalition agreements of rigorous cost-benefit analysis and basing decisions on data and evidence, and, if so, does he accept the advice of the International Energy Agency from 2021 that if Governments are serious about the climate crisis, there can be no new investments in oil, gas, and coal from now?
veracity.explanation: Relays a characterisation of the IEA's 2021 advice — that consistency with climate goals rules out new oil, gas and coal investment. What is checkable is whether the IEA said this, not whether it is correct.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IEA's 'Net Zero by 2050: A Roadmap for the Global Energy Sector' (May 2021); true if the report states that no new oil and gas fields approved for development and no new coal mines are required beyond 2021 in its net zero pathway, false if the report contains no such statement or is materially qualified against this characterisation.

specificity.statement: Why won’t the New Zealand Government call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire when more than 16,000 people have died, the great majority of them civilians, and that is continuing as we speak?
specificity.explanation: Names a precise policy ask (an immediate and permanent ceasefire) and attaches a numeric figure to the harm being cited; someone could check both.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve said, we would all like to see a sustainable ceasefire, but it actually requires all parties to actually make the conditions to make that happen, and for that to happen, for hostilities to cease, Hamas needs to actually cease its attacks on Israel, needs to stop exploiting civilian infrastructure and using civilians as shields, and it needs to locate and release all the remaining hostages.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete conditions (cease attacks, end use of civilian infrastructure, release hostages) rather than a generic call for peace, but supplies no timeframe or mechanism for achieving them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The official cash rate is at its highest level in 15 years, pushing mortgage interest rates over 7 percent.
specificity.explanation: A named instrument, a stated horizon and a numeric threshold — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Mr Robertson, it’s time for policies that back growth and investment, that reduce the tax burden on working people, and that restore discipline to Government spending, and that’s exactly what our Government will do.
specificity.explanation: Three directions of travel with no mechanism, no amount and no date. She was announcing an economic programme and could readily have supplied detail here.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update showed that New Zealand is expected to run a deficit of $11.4 billion this year.
specificity.explanation: Named source document, named year, exact figure — anyone can look it up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Dairy farmers across the country will be pleased with the news today that Fonterra have increased their forecast farm-gate milk price by 25c to $7.50—better times ahead.
specificity.explanation: Named company, named metric, the size of the movement and the resulting level.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are focused on three things: rebuilding the economy, restoring law and order, and delivering better outcomes for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Three broad headings, one of which ('better outcomes for New Zealanders') commits to nothing at all. No mechanism, target or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his commitment to remove the ban on new offshore oil and gas permits, and if so, does he agree with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment that a thorough analysis of the costs and benefits of removing the ban should be undertaken before any legislation is introduced?
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question: identifies the policy, the analysis sought and the point in the process at which it should occur.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re deeply committed to delivering on our climate change goals and commitments, but we believe that gas is better than coal.
specificity.explanation: A statement of commitment with no goal, target, date or mechanism named, plus a comparative assertion with no quantity attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes. I continue to seek advice from officials on the implementation of tax changes as part of the Budget process. I am still receiving advice on tax policies, and the details of any specific revenue measures the Government may choose to pursue are yet to be finalised.
specificity.explanation: Asked which specific revenue measures would fund the tax package, the answer supplies no measure, no amount and no date — the content is that details do not yet exist.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They will know in due course, and I’m sorry to say it, but I doubt that the member will be the first to know.
specificity.explanation: 'In due course' is the least checkable possible answer to a question that asked for a date; nothing here could be acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As I’ve said, we would all like to see a sustainable ceasefire, but it actually requires all parties to actually make the conditions to make that happen, and for that to happen, for hostilities to cease, Hamas needs to actually cease its attacks on Israel, needs to stop exploiting civilian infrastructure and using civilians as shields, and it needs to locate and release all the remaining hostages.
rigor.explanation: A conditional argument: a durable ceasefire requires conditions from both belligerents, and the conditions are then enumerated. The conclusion tracks the stated premises; no fallacy, though the necessity claim is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, yes, I have, and our Government might have inherited challenging economic conditions, but, clearly, our election has given many reason for hope, because ANZ’s Business Outlook shows business confidence is already higher than at any point during the last Government’s tenure. In fact, it’s at its highest level since March 2015.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: a rise in a survey reading following the election is treated as caused by the election. No mechanism or counterfactual is offered, and business confidence surveys routinely move on partisan lines regardless of policy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s very obvious to us that New Zealand needs transitionary energy sources, and gas is a good part to doing that.
rigor.explanation: The premise is asserted as self-evident ('very obvious to us') and the conclusion that gas specifically fills that role is offered with nothing to connect them — an appeal to obviousness in place of an argument, in direct response to a question about contrary expert analysis.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister as to whether or not the New Zealand Government—the new Government—added its name to the UN statement, and wouldn’t any informed member of Parliament in this country know that?
civility.explanation: The tail of the question is condescension aimed at the questioner rather than the substance — it implies the member asking is uninformed. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Net debt in the Pre-election Fiscal Update can be found in the Pre-election Fiscal Update, and I wonder if the member paid as much attention to that figure when he was spending New Zealanders’ hard-earned money with wild abandon, as he is today in this House.
civility.explanation: Sneering deflection that turns on the member personally — 'wild abandon' imputes recklessness and inattention to him rather than criticising a spending decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Could I ask the finance Minister as to whether or not all the recent economic and inflation evidence suggests that Labour on their own couldn’t run a proverbial in a you-know-what?
civility.explanation: Crude, but the target is a party rather than any individual; no person's character, competence or worth is attacked. Focus is where this fails, not Civility.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The difference between my approach and the previous Minister’s approach is I’m not hiding a sneaky wealth tax or capital gains tax when I answer these questions.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the member personally — 'sneaky', 'hiding' — rather than criticising a tax policy. A real failure short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They will know in due course, and I’m sorry to say it, but I doubt that the member will be the first to know.
civility.explanation: A mild personal jab at the member's standing rather than an answer, edging onto the person without landing a real insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is he concerned that under his watch, Aotearoa is failing to meet our legal obligations to act to prevent genocide, to protect the rights of children, and to act in the interests of global peace and security where war crimes are alleged—that’s “to act”?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the government's conduct against named legal obligations rather than on the other party's character; legitimate scrutiny of a policy position, though the obligations are cited in category terms rather than as a named instrument.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Previous promises made by the outgoing Minister of Finance to reduce Government spending after the pandemic—those promises were broken, with Government spending this financial year substantially higher than at any time during the pandemic, including periods where large parts of the country were locked down and businesses forcibly closed.
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment and a specific measurable outcome (spending levels against pandemic years). Holding a predecessor to a named fiscal commitment is on-policy accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I know that that member and many of her constituents understand that farmers remain the backbone of this country, and they finally have a Government that is committed to reducing the burden of regulation that was piled high by the previous one.
focus.explanation: There is a policy direction in here — regulatory burden on farmers — but no regulation, cost or measure is named, and the weight of the sentence is the contrast with the previous government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For six years, Kiwis have felt the pain as our country’s economy has crawled along under the weight of a red-tape loving, big spending, big-tech taxing, fiscally reckless Government, and I am proud to say that we now have a Government that is committed to getting our economy back on its feet.
focus.explanation: A string of epithets characterising the previous government's general disposition. No regulation, tax, spending line or figure is named — strip out the party framing and nothing about a policy remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could I ask the finance Minister as to whether or not all the recent economic and inflation evidence suggests that Labour on their own couldn’t run a proverbial in a you-know-what?
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or measure is named — the entire content is a generalised jeer at the other party's competence dressed as a question about 'evidence'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his commitment to remove the ban on new offshore oil and gas permits, and if so, does he agree with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment that a thorough analysis of the costs and benefits of removing the ban should be undertaken before any legislation is introduced?
focus.explanation: Names the specific policy (removing the offshore permit ban), the specific procedural question (cost-benefit analysis before legislation) and the authority advancing it. Entirely on the measure, not the party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On what date will New Zealanders know how she is paying for the tax cuts that she has promised them?
focus.explanation: Names the specific policy (the promised tax package) and asks for a specific, checkable thing — the date of disclosure. Textbook scrutiny of a named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In April 2021, the previous Government—screaming out now—approved $344 million to cover the full cost of the redevelopment of Scott Base, and in December 2022, an additional funding package was approved, bringing the total Government commitment to—listen to this—$503 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific Cabinet funding decisions for the Scott Base redevelopment: $344m approved in April 2021 and a further package in December 2022 taking the total commitment to $503m.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet minutes / Budget documents and Antarctica New Zealand annual reports for the Scott Base redevelopment; true if an April 2021 approval of ~$344m and a December 2022 top-up bringing total Crown commitment to ~$503m are recorded, false if the figures or dates differ materially.

veracity.statement: Does he acknowledge the deaths of over 16,000 Palestinians, more than 7,000 of whom are children, and that the disproportionate targeting of civilians can never constitute an exercise of the right to self-defence?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a casualty toll as at the date of the question: more than 16,000 Palestinians killed in Gaza, of whom more than 7,000 were children.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gaza Ministry of Health / UN OCHA reported cumulative Palestinian fatalities in Gaza as at 6–7 December 2023; true if the reported toll was at least 16,000 with at least 7,000 children, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Why is this Government attempting to cut courses, along with other Māori initiatives, then, that are designed to grow te reo speakers?
veracity.explanation: Presupposes as fact that the incoming coalition Government is moving to cut courses and other initiatives designed to grow te reo Māori speakers.
veracity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The 2022 Programme for International Student Assessment results released this week show a decline in the performance of 15-year-old students in maths compared to 2018 and confirm the long-term trend of declining achievement in core subjects.

veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD PISA 2022 country results for New Zealand (released 5 December 2023); true if NZ's mean mathematics score for 15-year-olds is lower than its PISA 2018 mean beyond the reported standard error, and if the reading/science series show a comparable long-run decline; false if the maths mean was flat or higher.

focus.statement: Why is this Government attempting to cut courses, along with other Māori initiatives, then, that are designed to grow te reo speakers?

civility.statement: The flow-on impacts to New Zealand and rest of the world of this scientific research is critically important, but the project must be completed in a cost-effective and timely manner which respects the hard-earned money of Kiwi taxpayers, and no more can outsiders think they can rip the taxpayer off because the people doing the auditing don’t know what they’re doing, like that man over there [Gestures to Hon Grant Robertson].
civility.explanation: Begins on the substance but ends by singling out a named individual across the Chamber as one of 'the people doing the auditing' who 'don’t know what they’re doing' — a direct attack on a member's personal competence rather than on the decision or the process.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Of course we acknowledge that, but we also wonder why there’s such an absence of the mass assault and massacre on 7 October this year. “Why are we hearing just one side of the story?”, is what a lot of people with balance and fairness want to know.
civility.explanation: Attributing the desire for balance and fairness to 'a lot of people' implies the questioner lacks both — an imputation of bad faith aimed at the member rather than at her argument, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: For a trained lawyer, coming to a conclusion on a case before you’ve heard the evidence laid out for you is not a sound way of behaving. That’s what a legal training means. You first hear the evidence and then, against the principles of precedent, we then make a decision. We’re not going to make a judgment without any facts before we come to that judgment.
civility.explanation: Opens by invoking the questioner's own profession to suggest she is behaving unprofessionally — a condescending lecture directed at the member personally rather than at the substance of what she asked.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No one in this House wants this conflict in the Middle East, but for a durable ceasefire to be viable, the parties must take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire. We recognise, again, that that point is not straightforward. Simply calling for a ceasefire does not make one a reality. That’s why we are calling on all parties and all countries with influence in the region to take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire now, permanently.
rigor.explanation: Near-circular: the conclusion ('we are calling on all parties to take urgent steps towards establishing a ceasefire') restates the premise. It also rests on an implied false dichotomy — that calling for a ceasefire and urging steps toward one are alternatives — which is what the inference needs to do the work of declining to join the call, and it is not established.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Of course we acknowledge that, but we also wonder why there’s such an absence of the mass assault and massacre on 7 October this year. “Why are we hearing just one side of the story?”, is what a lot of people with balance and fairness want to know.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque plus an appeal to popularity: the question about targeting of civilians is answered by pointing to a different set of atrocities, and the warrant offered is what 'a lot of people' are said to want to know. Neither supports the conclusion that the acknowledged conduct is defensible.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: For a trained lawyer, coming to a conclusion on a case before you’ve heard the evidence laid out for you is not a sound way of behaving. That’s what a legal training means. You first hear the evidence and then, against the principles of precedent, we then make a decision. We’re not going to make a judgment without any facts before we come to that judgment.
rigor.explanation: Despite the personal framing, the inference itself is sound and does not rest on the jibe: if determinations of breach require evidence assessed by a competent body, then declining to pronounce before that assessment follows. The contestable part (that no facts are yet available) is a factual premise, not a logical defect.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: As I said in answer to the primary question, which the member may not have listened to, yes, the tax reduction package promised by the Government in the Speech from the Throne will be self-funding. I’ll tell you what else it’ll do: it’ll put real cash into the bank accounts of working people—bank accounts that have been eroded by a cost of living crisis presided over by that member, who over-taxed them, spent their money badly, and left the economy in tatters.
civility.explanation: "which the member may not have listened to" is condescension aimed at the questioner, and "spent their money badly" turns the record criticism onto the member personally. Criticism of the previous government's fiscal record would itself be fine; the sneer is what costs.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How can he justify scrapping Aotearoa’s world-leading smoke-free laws, sacrificing Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy?
civility.explanation: "sacrificing Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy" imputes a callous motive to the Prime Minister rather than contesting the policy's effects. Bad faith imputed, short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Did he consider his obligations under the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control to keep tobacco industry influence out of Government before making the delegation to the Hon Casey Costello, who has previously chaired the Taxpayers’ Union, an organisation reported to receive funding from tobacco companies?
civility.explanation: Raises a conflict-of-interest question grounded in a named treaty obligation and a stated past role, which is legitimate scrutiny, but the guilt-by-association framing edges toward imputing bad faith to a named Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Was the 2022 target—smokefree at the end of 2025, which is not too many months away from now—ever zero smoking or 5 percent smoking, and what sort of fraud target is that?
civility.explanation: "what sort of fraud target is that" imputes dishonesty to whoever set the target, though it lands on the policy and the previous government rather than any named person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Did the Minister delegate responsibility for the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products Act because he doesn’t want to answer to the Cancer Society, the Stroke Foundation, the New Zealand Nurses Organisation, the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency, the Secondary Principals’ Council of New Zealand, and his own professional college, the College of General Practitioners, not to mention hundreds of other organisations that have condemned his actions?
civility.explanation: The question is built on an imputed motive — that the Minister delegated to avoid facing his critics and his own profession. That is an attribution of cowardice to the person, not a challenge to the decision's merits.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Labour’s pumped hydro scheme was a vanity project, and their intention to press ahead with it—no one cares about the project; that’s correct, Mr Jackson—was threatening the market-led investment needed to offer New Zealand the best chance of ensuring energy security.
civility.explanation: "vanity project" imputes ego to the other party's motives rather than contesting the scheme, but it lands on a party and a project, not on a named member.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I said in answer to the primary question, which the member may not have listened to, yes, the tax reduction package promised by the Government in the Speech from the Throne will be self-funding. I’ll tell you what else it’ll do: it’ll put real cash into the bank accounts of working people—bank accounts that have been eroded by a cost of living crisis presided over by that member, who over-taxed them, spent their money badly, and left the economy in tatters.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim (the tax package is self-funding, it raises take-home pay), but half the answer is a general characterisation of the opposing member's time in office rather than a named policy and outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, I do, and particularly our commitment to lifting educational achievement by removing distractions like cellphone use in the classroom to ensure that young people receive the quality education they deserve and lets them live the life that they ultimately want.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy — the classroom cellphone ban and educational achievement. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he stand by the decision to disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority, when it is an example of tangata whenua stepping up and being the solution to persistent inequalities in health outcomes?
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision and the agency being disestablished, and puts a reason for it. Scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he justify scrapping Aotearoa’s world-leading smoke-free laws, sacrificing Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy?
focus.explanation: Engages two named policies — the 2022 smokefree legislation and the tax package — rather than the other party in general. The "for the wealthy" framing is party rhetoric but the policy content dominates.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market. Fair pay agreements would reduce choice in workplaces and undermine the flexible labour market which has underpinned New Zealand’s economic success for the past three decades. Our Government believes the best way to introduce the wages of workers is to improve productivity and reduce regulations so businesses have more money to pay staff more.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure — what the law does, when it will be repealed, and what the Government proposes instead.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If any fair pay agreements were finalised, the increased costs would have greatly affected a range of businesses up and down the country, regardless of whether they could have afforded them. This would have increased prices for consumers and could cause business closures, which is worse for employees. I don’t consider that a blunt tool will help our labour markets for either employers or employees. Workers could have been negatively impacted, for example, if employers chose to hire fewer people or reduce hours of work due to higher costs that they face.
focus.explanation: Argues about the effects of the measure itself; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Was the 2022 target—smokefree at the end of 2025, which is not too many months away from now—ever zero smoking or 5 percent smoking, and what sort of fraud target is that?
focus.explanation: Engages a named policy target and its actual threshold — the Smokefree 2025 goal and whether it meant zero or 5 percent.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour’s pumped hydro scheme was a vanity project, and their intention to press ahead with it—no one cares about the project; that’s correct, Mr Jackson—was threatening the market-led investment needed to offer New Zealand the best chance of ensuring energy security.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim — that the scheme chilled market-led investment in generation — but it is wrapped in party framing and a mid-sentence jibe across the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I believe it’s over $60 million, but under that former Government, they don’t care about taxpayers’ money. They wasted money every single day on business cases, consultants, reports, and if they’d continued it would’ve been $8,000 per household, at least, for the $16 billion scheme they proposed.
focus.explanation: Real figures about a named scheme, but the weight of the answer is a general characterisation of the previous Government as not caring about taxpayers' money rather than the cost question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: As I said in answer to the primary question, which the member may not have listened to, yes, the tax reduction package promised by the Government in the Speech from the Throne will be self-funding. I’ll tell you what else it’ll do: it’ll put real cash into the bank accounts of working people—bank accounts that have been eroded by a cost of living crisis presided over by that member, who over-taxed them, spent their money badly, and left the economy in tatters.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the coalition's tax reduction package will be fiscally self-funding — paid for out of identified savings and revenue rather than additional borrowing.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget 2024 documents (Budget Economic and Fiscal Update and the tax package funding table): true if the package is fully funded from identified savings and new revenue measures with no attributable increase in forecast net core Crown debt; false if it is funded by additional borrowing or if the promised offsetting revenue measures do not eventuate.

specificity.statement: Yes, I do, and particularly our commitment to lifting educational achievement by removing distractions like cellphone use in the classroom to ensure that young people receive the quality education they deserve and lets them live the life that they ultimately want.
specificity.explanation: Names one concrete measure (removing cellphones from classrooms) but gives no timeframe, mechanism of enforcement, or achievement target.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the last decade, daily smoking’s gone from 16 percent down to 8 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two figures and a stated period; anyone can go to the Health Survey series and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market. Fair pay agreements would reduce choice in workplaces and undermine the flexible labour market which has underpinned New Zealand’s economic success for the past three decades. Our Government believes the best way to introduce the wages of workers is to improve productivity and reduce regulations so businesses have more money to pay staff more.
specificity.explanation: Names the law, the repeal, and the 100-day window, but the alternative ("improve productivity and reduce regulations") carries no mechanism, figure or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The current delegations I have given to the Associate Minister of Health, the Hon Costello, give effect to the coalition agreement with New Zealand First. I can assure the honourable member that the remaining delegations will be finalised shortly.
specificity.explanation: Names the delegate and the governing document, but neither identifies which delegations are outstanding nor gives a date — "shortly" commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did the Minister request his associate repeal a law that was shown, in modelling submitted to the select committee, would save over 8,000 lives, extend Māori life expectancy, and save billions in healthcare costs?
specificity.explanation: Names the source of the estimate, a figure for lives saved, and the categories of benefit — precise enough for someone to pull the select committee papers and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This week, I announced that the coalition Government had axed the former Government’s hugely wasteful $16 billion Lake Onslow scheme This decision fulfils another commitment under our coalition Government’s 100-day plan.
specificity.explanation: Names the scheme, the cost figure and the plan the decision sits under — all checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I believe it’s over $60 million, but under that former Government, they don’t care about taxpayers’ money. They wasted money every single day on business cases, consultants, reports, and if they’d continued it would’ve been $8,000 per household, at least, for the $16 billion scheme they proposed.
specificity.explanation: Gives a savings figure, a per-household figure and a total project cost, and names what the money went on. "I believe" hedges the first number but it remains checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, the first priority was to scrap this Lake Onslow scheme within our first hundred days. Our next steps are to cut the red tape and to recognise the nature of the energy problem facing our country so that we can double renewable energy by 2050. Axing the Lake Onslow scheme and our coalition Government’s commitments to allow natural gas to function as a transition fuel will give our energy sector much greater confidence to invest in the dry year solution and keep the lights on.
specificity.explanation: One concrete target with a date (double renewable energy by 2050) and a named transition-fuel commitment, but "cut the red tape" and "recognise the nature of the energy problem" name no regulation, mechanism or step.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have not committed to a referendum.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the coalition Government has made no commitment to hold a referendum on the Treaty principles, as distinct from taking a Treaty Principles Bill to select committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT and National–NZ First coalition agreements of 24 November 2023: true if neither document commits the Government to a referendum on the Treaty principles, false if either does.

veracity.statement: In the last decade, daily smoking’s gone from 16 percent down to 8 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts adult daily smoking prevalence in New Zealand halved over roughly the decade to 2023, from about 16 percent to about 8 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey adult daily smoking prevalence, 2012/13 compared with the most recent year available at December 2023: true if the two figures are approximately 16% and 8% (within rounding), false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: I agree with my statement, and I also agree with the recommendations from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s (MBIE’s) regulatory impact statement before the fair pay agreements legislation was passed, where MBIE recommended against introducing fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MBIE's regulatory impact statement on the fair pay agreements legislation recommended against introducing the regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE regulatory impact statement accompanying the Fair Pay Agreements Bill (2021–22): true if its preferred option was not to introduce fair pay agreements or it advised against the proposal; false if it recommended the regime or was neutral.

veracity.statement: Why did the Minister request his associate repeal a law that was shown, in modelling submitted to the select committee, would save over 8,000 lives, extend Māori life expectancy, and save billions in healthcare costs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that modelling put before the select committee on the 2022 smokefree legislation projected over 8,000 lives saved, gains in Māori life expectancy, and health system savings in the billions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The modelling submitted to the Health Select Committee on the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Bill and its published counterparts: true if a projection of ≥8,000 deaths averted, increased Māori life expectancy, and health-system savings of ≥NZ$1 billion appears there; false if the published estimates are materially smaller or absent.

veracity.statement: Did he consider his obligations under the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control to keep tobacco industry influence out of Government before making the delegation to the Hon Casey Costello, who has previously chaired the Taxpayers’ Union, an organisation reported to receive funding from tobacco companies?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Casey Costello previously chaired the New Zealand Taxpayers' Union and that the organisation has been reported to receive tobacco industry funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Taxpayers' Union governance records and contemporaneous media reporting: true if Costello held the chair of the Taxpayers' Union and published reporting documents tobacco company funding of that organisation; false if she never chaired it or no such funding reporting exists.

veracity.statement: The target itself, through all the documents I’ve seen, was unlikely to be achieved even with that Government’s proposed policies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official advice and analysis indicated the Smokefree 2025 target would not be met even under the previous Government's tobacco endgame policies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Health advice and the published modelling of the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022: true if that analysis projected the daily smoking target would not be reached by end-2025 under those policies; false if it projected the target would be reached.

veracity.statement: This week, I announced that the coalition Government had axed the former Government’s hugely wasteful $16 billion Lake Onslow scheme This decision fulfils another commitment under our coalition Government’s 100-day plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme carried a cost of $16 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Battery Project business case cost estimates for the Lake Onslow pumped hydro option: true if the published capital cost estimate is approximately $16 billion, false if the estimate is materially lower or no such figure was published.

veracity.statement: Yes. I have also seen a report in The Press today where Labour’s energy spokesperson, and the former Minister for Energy and Resources, has said that Labour is rethinking its policy on this scheme.
veracity.explanation: Relays a media report that Labour's energy spokesperson said the party is reconsidering its position on the Lake Onslow scheme.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Press, 7 December 2023: true if the article reports Labour's energy spokesperson saying the party is rethinking its policy on the Lake Onslow pumped hydro scheme; false if no such article or statement exists.

rigor.statement: How can he justify scrapping Aotearoa’s world-leading smoke-free laws, sacrificing Māori lives to fund tax cuts for the wealthy?
rigor.explanation: The inference from "repealing the smokefree laws" to "funding tax cuts with Māori lives" is asserted, not shown: no link is offered between the tobacco excise revenue and the tax package, and the conclusion is a false-dilemma framing of two separate decisions.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: ACT and National are both strongly opposed to fair pay agreements. When the law was introduced, both parties opposed it, and both campaigned to repeal it in the first 100 days of this Government. As a Government, we are committed to acting quickly to remove this law before any fair pay agreements are finalised and the negative impacts are felt by the labour market. Fair pay agreements would reduce choice in workplaces and undermine the flexible labour market which has underpinned New Zealand’s economic success for the past three decades. Our Government believes the best way to introduce the wages of workers is to improve productivity and reduce regulations so businesses have more money to pay staff more.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that fair pay agreements would undermine the labour market rests on a post hoc attribution — three decades of economic success are credited to labour market flexibility, with nothing offered to establish that link or to show the Act would break it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If any fair pay agreements were finalised, the increased costs would have greatly affected a range of businesses up and down the country, regardless of whether they could have afforded them. This would have increased prices for consumers and could cause business closures, which is worse for employees. I don’t consider that a blunt tool will help our labour markets for either employers or employees. Workers could have been negatively impacted, for example, if employers chose to hire fewer people or reduce hours of work due to higher costs that they face.
rigor.explanation: The chain from higher labour costs to prices, closures and reduced hours is internally coherent and the mechanism is spelled out, but every step is asserted with no evidence, and "regardless of whether they could have afforded them" is stated rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The target itself, through all the documents I’ve seen, was unlikely to be achieved even with that Government’s proposed policies.
rigor.explanation: Leans entirely on an appeal to unnamed documents "I've seen" — no source, figure or projection is offered, so the conclusion cannot be traced back to anything the House can weigh.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But it’s New Zealand’s first MMP coalition with three parties in it, and I think it’s worth reflecting on that, because there are a lot of people, particularly during the interregnum period—and members opposite won’t necessarily say this publicly, but I reckon I’m right in saying that they enjoyed the break from being in Parliament and enjoyed the break from their ministerial boxes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2023 National–ACT–NZ First arrangement is the first government under MMP formed as a coalition of three parties, as distinct from earlier two-party coalitions supported by confidence-and-supply partners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of government formation agreements since 1996 (party coalition agreements and ministerial appointments): true if no MMP government before 2023 had three parties bound by coalition agreements with ministers inside the executive; false if an earlier MMP government did (e.g. if a confidence-and-supply arrangement is counted as coalition membership).

veracity.statement: We’ve seen the outcome of more Government. We’ve seen what a ginormous increase in Government spending does, like we saw over the last six years. We have the official cash rate at the highest it has been since 2008. We have ever-increasing debt. We have deficits as far as the eye can see.
veracity.explanation: Within the passage, the checkable assertion is that the official cash rate stood at its highest level since 2008 as at December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand official cash rate series: true if the OCR prevailing in December 2023 exceeds every OCR level recorded between 2009 and 2023; false if the OCR was higher at any point in that period.

focus.statement: And I think it speaks to everything that the Labour Party thinks about Government and about Parliament: that we have to spend more money, we have to do things, set up a new Government programme.
focus.explanation: Characterises what the Labour Party as a party 'thinks' rather than engaging a measure before the House. There is a sliver of policy content (spending, new programmes) but no named policy, figure or outcome, so the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And that’s why this Government is committed to cutting red tape and investing in productivity-enhancing infrastructure to get Government out of the way and let Kiwis get on with their lives.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the Government intends to do in policy terms — regulation and infrastructure — rather than about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve seen the outcome of more Government. We’ve seen what a ginormous increase in Government spending does, like we saw over the last six years. We have the official cash rate at the highest it has been since 2008. We have ever-increasing debt. We have deficits as far as the eye can see.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about a real policy: the increase in government spending is offered as the cause of the current OCR, debt and deficit position. The reasoning is single-cause/post hoc — the listed outcomes are presented as following from spending alone, with nothing offered to exclude the global inflation shock, the pandemic response or monetary policy settings as causes.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: And that’s why this Government is committed to cutting red tape and investing in productivity-enhancing infrastructure to get Government out of the way and let Kiwis get on with their lives.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel with no mechanism, no amount, no timeframe and no named regulation or project. 'Cutting red tape' and 'productivity-enhancing infrastructure' are not checkable or actionable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The books bequeathed to us by Grant Robertson and the Labour Party are not in good shape, and over the next few weeks and months, and probably beyond that as well, we will be doing an exposure exercise to show to the New Zealand people just what a shoddy job the last Government did and what a terrible situation the incoming Government inherits.
civility.explanation: Harsh about the previous Government's fiscal record — 'shoddy job', 'terrible situation' — but the target throughout is the record and the state of the accounts, not Grant Robertson's character, competence or worth. Naming the former Minister as the author of the books is attribution, not an attack on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There’s one good thing about the Government opposite, and that is that the member who’s just resumed his seat has not taken on the role of Minister of Finance, because we’ve discovered in the last week or so that he can’t tell the difference between the number one and the number 35.
civility.explanation: A clear personal attack: the point is delivered as a deficiency in a named member's numeracy and fitness for office, not as criticism of a policy. There was a civil version of this available (state the figures and the error), so the opportunity to score across the scale was real.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That tells you all you need to know about Mr Bishop’s mathematical ability and, sadly, also about this Government.
civility.explanation: Generalises a single disputed figure into a verdict on a named member's competence. The target is the person's ability, not the argument or the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Or when Brooke van Velden decides to incorrectly and misleadingly represent the views of Simon Upton, that apparently also is not part of it.
civility.explanation: 'Decides to ... misleadingly represent' imputes deliberate bad faith to a named member rather than alleging a mistake. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes intent to deceive to the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’ve got news for Christopher Luxon: your circus, your clowns.
civility.explanation: Calls the members of the governing parties clowns — abuse aimed at people, with no argument attached.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Chris Bishop seems to think that the outcome of the previous Government’s smoke-free changes was that there would be one outlet in all of Northland selling cigarettes, when in actual fact the publicly available number was 35.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable things: that Bishop publicly claimed the smoke-free retailer changes would leave one outlet in Northland, and that the published allocation for Northland was 35.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Health / Health NZ published regional allocation of approved smoked-tobacco retailers under the Smokefree Environments and Regulated Products (Smoked Tobacco) Amendment Act 2022: true if the published Northland figure is 35, false if it is one or a materially different number. Bishop's side of it settles on the record of his public statements in the week before 7 December 2023: true if he stated one outlet for Northland, false if he did not.

veracity.statement: When Winston Peters calls the Public Interest Journalism Fund bribery, accuses the media of accepting bribes, goes on weird rants about conspiracy theories about the World Health Organization and how they’re going to run New Zealand, apparently Mr Luxon says, “No, that is not me.”, unlike Chris Bishop.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Peters characterised the Public Interest Journalism Fund as bribery and made claims about the World Health Organization running New Zealand, and that Luxon publicly distanced himself from such remarks. The characterisation 'weird rants' is rhetoric, but the underlying attributions are matters of record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of Winston Peters' statements in late 2023 (press conferences, media reports, Hansard): true if he described the Public Interest Journalism Fund as bribery or a bribe and made public claims about the WHO's authority over New Zealand; false if no such statements exist. Luxon's side settles on reported comments where he declined to endorse Peters' wording.

specificity.statement: Chris Bishop seems to think that the outcome of the previous Government’s smoke-free changes was that there would be one outlet in all of Northland selling cigarettes, when in actual fact the publicly available number was 35.
specificity.explanation: Names the person, the policy, the region and two competing figures, and points at where the correct one is published. Someone could go and check it without asking a further question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am proud to be part of a Labour Party that achieved a lot over the last six years that we were in Government.
specificity.explanation: Claims six years of achievement without naming one policy, figure, programme or outcome, and the surrounding sentences supply none either. Nothing here is checkable or actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think Nicola Willis wants to go backwards to 1993—she wants to go back 30 years—to the last years of Ruth Richardson, where the cuts to public services were deep, where New Zealand communities right around the country felt the effect of a Government who didn’t care, a Government who cut the services that they need.
focus.explanation: A debate on the coalition agreements, and this engages none of them: it attributes a private wish to an opponent and characterises a government of thirty years ago. No measure, figure, commitment or outcome in the agreements before the House is named, so there is nothing here that could be held to account.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If New Zealand wants to sell its goods into the world, we have to be doing the right thing by our planet. Every single exporter in New Zealand knows that.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question — the link between climate action and export markets — rather than on the other parties. Scores high here despite the weak support, which is the intended focus/rigor split.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Kieran McAnulty said it very well in this House last night: the problem that lot have with the Māori Health Authority isn’t the last two words; it’s the first word.
focus.explanation: A named policy — the Māori Health Authority — but the content is a claim about opponents' motives rather than about the authority's performance, cost or design. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If New Zealand wants to sell its goods into the world, we have to be doing the right thing by our planet. Every single exporter in New Zealand knows that.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to unanimity ('every single exporter knows that') rather than on anything showing that overseas buyers actually condition purchases on emissions performance. The claim may well be right; nothing offered here establishes it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Look, I’m happy to offer the previous speaker my pocket square, because he has a large dollop of sad sauce right there on his face.
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at Grant Robertson — mocking his demeanour and appearance rather than engaging anything he argued. Not sustained abuse, but it lands on the person, not the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have resoundingly told us here in this House that the Labour Government was a failure.
focus.explanation: A blanket verdict on the other party with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. This is party framing rather than scrutiny of a specific commitment. Rigor is deliberately not scored here: strip out the characterisation of Labour and no argument remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because these were people who really wanted to get ahead and, in many instances, it was around housing-related issues—and we’ve seen that wait-list for public housing go through the roof, an extra 20,000-odd under the previous Government, despite them saying that housing was going to be one of their key solutions that they first came in on.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: it names a specific policy area, a specific commitment the previous government made, and a specific numeric outcome. Holding a government to a named commitment is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We saw Kiwis up and down New Zealand changing their minds at the polls, and thank goodness they did, because there are so many examples, so many cases of this country going backwards. I heard it consistently in the mighty Waikato on the campaign trail. People were worried that their groceries cost too much, that their kids weren’t learning what they should be at school, that their parents couldn’t get the hospital care they needed, and that the local dairy kept getting ripped off.
rigor.explanation: A real inference about real policy areas (cost of living, schooling, hospital access, retail crime), but the support offered is an appeal to anecdote plus an appeal to the election result — what he heard on the campaign trail is used to establish that the country was going backwards. No data or mechanism connects the reports to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Because these were people who really wanted to get ahead and, in many instances, it was around housing-related issues—and we’ve seen that wait-list for public housing go through the roof, an extra 20,000-odd under the previous Government, despite them saying that housing was going to be one of their key solutions that they first came in on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the public housing wait-list grew by roughly 20,000 applicants over the 2017–2023 Labour government's term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development Housing Register quarterly statistics: compare the number of applicants on the public housing register at the end of 2017 with the figure at the most recent quarter before December 2023. True if the net increase is approximately 20,000 applicants; false if the increase is materially smaller (or if the register fell).

veracity.statement: And we can see that with the few significant infrastructure projects the last Government put forward, none of which actually commenced or progressed at all.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no significant infrastructure project put forward by the 2017–2023 Labour government commenced or progressed. Extracted as an absolute, checkable claim about the past — the hyperbole is what makes it checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Enumerate the major infrastructure projects advanced by the 2017–2023 government (e.g. Transmission Gully, Pūhoi to Warkworth, City Rail Link, Te Huia, the Waikato Expressway sections) and check NZTA / KiwiRail / City Rail Link Ltd construction and completion records. False if any of them commenced construction or advanced to a later stage during that term; true only if none did.

veracity.statement: Our productivity has continued to decline for some time and now we are focusing on addressing that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's productivity has been declining — not merely growing slowly — over the period preceding December 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ productivity statistics (measured-sector labour productivity and multifactor productivity indexes) for the years up to the March 2023 year. True if the index level fell across those years; false if productivity levels rose, i.e. if only the growth rate slowed rather than the level declining.

specificity.statement: And I do just want to touch briefly on health, because in the Waikato we will be in our first 100 days signing a memorandum of understanding with the University of Waikato about establishing a third medical school.
specificity.explanation: A named counterparty, a named instrument (memorandum of understanding), a named objective (a third medical school) and a stated timeframe (the first 100 days). Someone could check whether it happened. No cost or student numbers, which is what keeps it off 1.0.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have a Government now—a coalition Government—that is ambitious for New Zealand again, that has a plan and will actually deliver outcomes.
specificity.explanation: Asserts ambition, a plan and delivery without naming the plan, any measure, any figure or any date. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What people don’t realise: manufacturing accounts for 230,000 people employed in this economy—230,000 people; about 10 percent of the economy. It underpins about two-thirds of the value of all our exports.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three figures about the NZ manufacturing sector as at late 2023: headcount employed (230,000), its share of the economy (~10 percent), and its share of export value (~two-thirds).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Business Employment Data / HLFS employment in the manufacturing industry and Stats NZ national accounts manufacturing share of GDP for 2023, plus MBIE/Stats NZ merchandise export composition; true if manufacturing employment is near 230,000, GDP share near 10 percent, and manufactured goods are around two-thirds of export value; false if any figure is materially outside those ranges (e.g. export share nearer half).

veracity.statement: I know when I employed lots of people, to be able to budget for increases in minimum wage—and we used to do roughly about 50c when we were last in Government every year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous National-led government raised the statutory adult minimum wage by approximately 50 cents an hour in each year it was in office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MBIE record of adult minimum wage rates for each 1 April increase from 2009 to 2017; true if the annual increases average around 50c with most years at or near that figure, false if the typical annual increase is materially lower (e.g. clustered at 25c).

specificity.statement: What people don’t realise: manufacturing accounts for 230,000 people employed in this economy—230,000 people; about 10 percent of the economy. It underpins about two-thirds of the value of all our exports.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, checkable quantities — a headcount, a share of the economy and a share of export value — attached to a named sector.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our objectives are to provide stability. We want to grow economic prosperity, because when you do, that means everyone in New Zealand benefits—everyone. We want to restore national unity, and that’s probably going to be the hardest thing to do, with all the division we’ve got. And we’re going to boost social cohesiveness alongside the rights and responsibility of being a New Zealand citizen.
specificity.explanation: A list of generic virtues — stability, prosperity, unity, cohesion — with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re going to repeal that dreadful proposal, the fair pay agreement, by Christmas.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific measure to be repealed and gives a deadline; anyone can check whether it happened by that date.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We want to grow economic prosperity, because when you do, that means everyone in New Zealand benefits—everyone.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that growth benefits literally everyone is asserted, not argued: no mechanism of distribution is offered, and the sweeping universal generalisation (repeated as 'everyone') is exactly what would need supporting.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Unfortunately, that Labour Government over there, for the last six years, just saw them as a cash tool and they imposed heaps of regulation on them without properly considering the nature and the cost and the burden of that regulation on small businesses. That is why New Zealand is in such a parlous state.
rigor.explanation: Single-cause fallacy: regulatory burden on small businesses is offered as the whole explanation for the state of the national economy, with no evidence connecting the two and no other cause considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We want to reintroduce the 90-day trials, because we believe that is a good way—in fact, an enhancing way to get people who you are going to take a risk on, to see if they can work in your factory.
rigor.explanation: The reason given for the policy is the speaker's own belief that it is 'a good way' — a bare assertion restating the conclusion rather than evidence that 90-day trials increase hiring of marginal candidates.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Unfortunately, that Labour Government over there, for the last six years, just saw them as a cash tool and they imposed heaps of regulation on them without properly considering the nature and the cost and the burden of that regulation on small businesses. That is why New Zealand is in such a parlous state.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — the compliance burden of regulation on small business — but carried mostly by characterisation of the other party's motives ('a cash tool') rather than by naming a specific regulation or cost.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re going to have an inquiry into the banking competition. We’re going to expand the role of the Grocery Commissioner. We’re going to rewrite that dreadful credit contracts and consumer finance Act that that Government there implemented.
focus.explanation: Three named policy actions — a banking competition inquiry, the Grocery Commissioner's remit, and the CCCFA — with the only party framing being a passing 'that Government there'.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is a clear signal from this new Government that they do not intend to take the environment or climate change seriously, because it conflicts with their policy agenda, which is largely about representing vested interests who want to maintain the status quo.
rigor.explanation: A real inference from a real premise (the environment and climate portfolios sit outside Cabinet) to a conclusion about intent, but the leap from ministerial ranking to 'do not intend to take it seriously' and thence to imputed motive is unsupported — the conclusion outruns what the premise shows.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They don’t understand that it’s possible to have economically rational investment that improves people’s options to alternatives, but the reality is—and we have 50 years of data on this if any of the members opposite would like to see it—that urban motorways do not reduce congestion; they make it worse; that the billions of dollars spent in central Wellington on an extra lane, an extra kilometre of lane is not going to make it easier to get to the airport; and that those billions of dollars spent in central Wellington and on the fringe of Auckland, and in Christchurch, are billions of dollars that this National-led Government will not be spending on the rural roads in the regions that actually need investment.
rigor.explanation: The opportunity-cost step (money spent on urban motorways is money not spent on rural roads) follows cleanly, and induced demand is a real mechanism. But the central empirical claim leans on '50 years of data' that is gestured at and never produced — an appeal to unproduced evidence carrying the weight of the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Perhaps it’s because the direct beneficiaries of these highways are the greenfields land bankers who probably donated to all three of these parties, and that is the truth.
rigor.explanation: The explanation is offered as speculation ('perhaps', 'probably') and then asserted as established fact ('that is the truth'). Nothing connects the premise to the conclusion — no donation record, no named beneficiary — so it is a bare imputation of motive dressed as a causal account.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve got to say that is someone going back in time, I think, and I think I’d just say to the Hon Julie Anne Genter, maybe she should come up to Franklin, just south of Auckland, and try and get on the motorway and drive to work at 6.30 in the morning and tell all those people who are struggling to get on the motorway, let alone drive along the motorway, because it’s absolutely congested, that they are ignorant fools, because I’m not sure that they’re going to agree with you.
rigor.explanation: Two defects. It answers an empirical claim about whether motorway expansion relieves congestion with a single anecdote about morning congestion in Franklin — an appeal to anecdote that does not bear on the claim. And it strawmans: Genter called the Government ignorant fools, not commuters, so the rebuttal is aimed at a position she did not take.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think many people out of Wellington CBD, because that’s where you seem to put your focus, would find that it’s particularly out in the rural communities where we do need to see a lot more infrastructure investment.
rigor.explanation: On the policy question of where investment should go, but the support offered is an appeal to what 'many people' would think — unnamed and unquantified — combined with a suggestion that the opposing view is merely parochial. No evidence connects the premise to the conclusion about rural need.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In both Wellington Central and Rongotai, I am happy to say that the Green Party won the party vote.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Green Party took the largest share of the party vote in both the Wellington Central and Rongotai electorates at the 2023 general election.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission official 2023 general election party-vote results by electorate; true if the Green Party has the highest party-vote total in both Wellington Central and Rongotai, false if any other party leads in either.

veracity.statement: New Zealand’s tax system has ranked 136 th out of 162 countries for promoting equity—that is the reality.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a cross-country index of tax systems' contribution to equity places New Zealand 136th of 162.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Identify the index referred to (most likely the Oxfam/DFI Commitment to Reducing Inequality Index, which ranks ~158–162 countries on a progressive-taxation pillar); true if New Zealand's taxation-pillar rank in the edition current in December 2023 is 136 of 162, false if the rank or denominator materially differ or no such index ranking exists.

veracity.statement: We see it in the United States, where 50 million people can’t afford healthcare, and they’re spending more money on prisons.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that about 50 million people in the United States cannot afford healthcare. The second clause ('spending more money on prisons') has no stated comparator and is not part of the checkable claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: US Census Bureau uninsured counts and KFF/Commonwealth Fund survey estimates of adults reporting they went without needed care because of cost, for the period around 2023; true if a defensible figure of roughly 50 million (±20%) can be supported on either measure, false if the best available figures are materially lower.

veracity.statement: Not even $500 million was spent in the entirety of Northland on roads over the 11-year period—nine years of that was under the National Government, and they are planning to spend over $2 billion for an extra kilometre lane in central Wellington because they believe that it will make it 30 seconds faster for them to drive from the airport to the Beehive.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that under $500 million was spent on roads in Northland over an 11-year period, nine years of it under a National government, and (b) that the incoming Government plans to spend over $2 billion on roughly one extra kilometre of lane in central Wellington.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) NZTA/Waka Kotahi National Land Transport Programme regional expenditure for Northland, roughly 2012–2023; true if total roading spend is under $500 million, false if materially above. (b) National's 2023 transport policy costings and NZTA business cases for the Wellington projects (second Mount Victoria tunnel / Basin Reserve); true if the committed spend exceeds $2 billion for approximately one additional lane-kilometre.

veracity.statement: We are having to spend $500 million extra on fixing up some of the potholes—won’t fix it all.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the incoming Government is committing an additional $500 million to road pothole repair.
veracity.subject: speaker
